title: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
author: Stevie Bonifield
text:
CEO Sam Altman said recently that OpenAI is prioritizing safety instead of going ‘guns blazing’ toward an IPO.﻿

CEO Sam Altman said recently that OpenAI is prioritizing safety instead of going ‘guns blazing’ toward an IPO.﻿

OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg . That would make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion.

Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects .

OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

title: The Guardian view on the AI backlash: American voters want a say in their future | Editorial
author: Editorial
text:
Tech stocks have lost trillions while voters have rejected the industry’s political champions. The billionaire-led boom is facing a democratic reckoning

This week’s midterms showed that the political bill for the AI boom is falling due. The Democratic sweep intensified fears over runaway spending, mounting debt and resistance to datacentres, sending tech shares tumbling. On Thursday Wall Street suffered its worst day since the pandemic as $3.2tn was wiped from markets. Anthropic, developer of the Claude chatbot, is hoping to float within the next fortnight for $1.5tn (£1.1tn), but it may not now get even a trillion dollars. The dominant AI chipmaker Nvidia saw its value crash by more than $400bn. The world’s richest man, Elon Musk, lost $113bn in two days .

While a few very rich people may be a little less wealthy, the sell-off may not be a bad thing. It brings a needed dose of reality to an industry whose spending plans and valuations depend on heroic expectations of future profits. That is a view held by many influential figures – from Goldman Sachs’ research boss to Nobel laureate Daron Acemoğlu . AI may transform the economy. That does not guarantee investors will earn back the sums being poured into it.

title: Mark Lynskey Opens Up About the Tragic Toll Behind the Bankruptcy
author: Josh Ross
text:
Mark Lynskey is famous for not speaking to the press, but today, that streak comes to an end. Following the April 30th Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing of Lynskey Performance Products, he has gone on record with Bicycle Retailer and Industry News to explain the profound personal losses that brought the storied brand to where it is today.

The Lynskey family has deep, respected roots in American titanium manufacturing. After launching Litespeed in 1986 and selling the brand in 1999, the family made a triumphant return to the industry in 2006 under the Lynskey Performance banner. Operating out of Chattanooga, Tennessee, the company quickly established a highly regarded domestic fabrication facility.

However, Lynskey reveals that the company’s recent unraveling was triggered by a tragic and severe leadership vacuum. Over the last few years, the brand suffered the deaths of plant manager Steve Kirby, head machinist Bill Thompson, veteran welder Louis Scroggins, and eventually, co-founder David Lynskey.

This cascading loss of institutional knowledge devastated management and production. In response, the company pivoted to heavily discounted direct-to-consumer and eBay sales. That shift in turn alienated its established dealer network, compounded existing supply chain gridlock, and ultimately forced the Chapter 11 filing.

Sitting down with Dean Yobbi to discuss the human toll behind the headlines, Lynskey remains focused on the future: “As a family, we are dedicated to bringing this brand back to what it represents.”

To see the numbers behind the reorganization, the company’s current operating status, and its strategy to rebuild dealer trust, read the complete feature at Bicycle Retailer .

title: Winners & losers from F1 2026 Brazilian GP Friday practice
author: Ben Anderson
text:
A familiar name at the top of the timesheet, but not your run of the mill F1 Friday at the Brazilian Grand Prix, as one struggling frontrunner got back in the groove again while the usual kings of Friday practice produced their worst result of the season.

Here are our winners and losers from the first day of F1 track action at Interlagos.

Loser: Ferrari (6th & 7th)

Charles Leclerc and Ferrari had been fastest in Friday practice at three of the past four races, going back to October’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and a 6-7 FP2 result in Brazil (with Leclerc behind Lewis Hamilton) was the first time all season Ferrari has finished Friday outside the top five on the timesheet. Leclerc called it a “very, very difficult Friday” and described the feeling inside the car as “strange” and “very poor”.

“We were losing in the straights, but I think the car in the corners just felt probably one of the worst Friday feelings of the season," he added.

“So I think there's a lot to be found in corners, more than in the straights, where we know we have a deficit. Normally we are very fast in corners and today was not the case.”

Team boss Fred Vasseur joked this was a Friday when Ferrari “have 200 kilos” of fuel inside the cars in order to flip the script, such is their usually prodigious form in free practice, but in a serious moment then admitted Ferrari has “a lot of work to do on the balance”.

“The drivers, they were not happy,” he confirmed, while also saying he was “not less optimistic than last week” when Leclerc topped Friday in Mexico.

“We had a couple of times a deployment issue in the lap,” Vasseur added. “We have to fine-tune everything.

“On his fastest lap, he [Leclerc] lost a couple of tenths in a straight line. I would say that it’s not a drama. It’s more for you [the media] to be focused on page one [of the timing screen], but we are not.

“We know that we have a lot to do on the balance. The balance was not good. The tarmac is the opposite of one week ago. It’s creating a lot of work to do and a difference compared to last week.” -

Winner: McLaren (2nd & 5th)

Fastest in FP1 and looking competitive on longer runs - McLaren's upgrade package for Brazil appears to be working well, with the usual caveat that Fridays don't always offer perfect insight into the order. Senior racing director Randy Singh said it's "very likely" the upgrades - led by a new front wing - will stay on the car, and Friday went "really well" for the team, while Lando Norris cautioned that the team still looks two-tenths off Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes but "pretty good" compared to the other teams.

Norris also felt gently encouraged that McLaren's new 2027-ethos front wing had begun to address the long-standing edginess of the car's balance.

"I would say maybe there’s a small change in the right direction, that it seems just a little bit more straightforward to drive," he said.

"I don’t think we can ever judge things over just one track. But so far, for today, things have seemed a little bit more straightforward." After missing FP1, Singh says Oscar Piastri was also "immediately on the pace" - something which hasn't always happened this year - but the usual rule from recent races applies: the team needs to optimise qualifying, where its knife-edge car has let its long-run pace down all too often. -

Winner: Gabriele Mini (7th in FP1)

Every now and then, a lesser-known Friday driver pops up high on the timesheets in an FP1 outing, which is exactly what Gabriele Mini did on his second appearance for Alpine by setting the seventh-fastest time to head the midfield pack.

"Gabby did a very good job to be a little bit quicker than his team-mate," said Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen.

"[It's the] second weekend in a row for him and he looks like a seasoned campaigner already. He literally didn't put a foot wrong, which is really good."

The 21-year-old Italian, when he wasn't reading from the standard FP1 driver script about focusing on doing a good job for the team, showed that he wasn't keen to rest on his laurels after making a positive impression and admitted to areas where he knew his lap, quick as it was, could have been better.

"There were a few things that, let’s say, didn’t allow me to make the best lap," said Mini when asked by The Race to break down his lap.

"The lap of your life, it’s really hard to get in an FP1, but where I had some margin was in corners like Turn 1, because there was never a clear run before the actual push, so I never really had an idea, so I took a bit of margin there, which I know I have.

"And then some other corners, a bit in the braking points, some slides that I got that could have been better. It’s hard to really say how much time. I don’t [say] one second, but for sure a few tenths are easy.

"Something that we could have done better with the switches as well, so not only my side. But that’s something that, as I said, you get in FP1 to then improve in FP2, both driver- and engineer-wise. So it’s normal to have those kinds of things, I’d say."

Mini, who was a star name in his karting career and has since won the 2020 Italian F4 title and races at every level up to and including F2, has shown that not only is he quick but also determined to improve.

And those are two key prerequisites of a potential F1 race driver. -

Loser: Anyone hoping Kimi Antonelli would switch off...

For anyone unfamiliar with old English idioms, something ‘after the Lord Mayor’s Show’ is a classic expression to describe something mundane, or disappointment following something much grander – like, for instance, a bog-standard F1 Friday for Kimi Antonelli five days after winning the world championship!

But anyone hoping Antonelli would be switching off with some kind of post-title hangover will be sorely disappointed by how he breezed through practice at Interlagos with all his rivals at arm’s length.

"It’s the next Lord Mayor’s show for him, not the after," said Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord.

"There’s two big things. We’ve got our constructors’ championship to win and a job to complete, and both drivers are really determined to do that, to translate and recognise the effort of everyone back in Brixworth and in Brackley.

"And then this is the start of 2027 for Kimi, and he’s determined to finish the season on a high, but take that momentum through into the winter."

There is no hint of complacency, change in mindset, or relaxing off the gas for the new world champion.

Without him, Mercedes would have looked right in the mix against McLaren and Red Bull, but nothing more. With Antonelli it heads into Saturday as the pole favourite - if the weather doesn’t change, of course. -

Winner: Colton Herta (20th in FP1)

It looks like Colton Herta has really, genuinely, finally done it – he qualifies for an F1 superlicence, in one of the most unnecessary and dragged-out driver eligibility storylines of all time.

Herta needed to rack up 100km in FP1, and avoid any licence penalty points, to get the one bonus superlicence point required to finally hit the threshold he and Cadillac thought he’d reached a week ago in Mexico.

That basically meant 23 laps of Interlagos. Herta’s credited with 31, which is well past the kilometre threshold – although, as Cadillac’s Marc Hynes mentioned, there’s a tiny degree of doubt whether you count only timed laps or just what’s logged in the session.

By our count, Herta managed 23 timed laps that were not inlaps or outlaps, so we reckoned he should be safe. Hynes said 24 was the “sweet spot”, but this just means being absolutely 100% sure either way.

And Herta avoided any sanction in-session that would deny him the bonus superlicence, after a near-miss not coming into the pits when the session was red flagged because he was too close to the pit entry to react when the panels lit up. Phew!

The FIA subsequently confirmed that Herta’s now all good, so this is now something that everybody, especially him, can stop worrying about... -

Winner: Gabriel Bortoleto’s Audi (8th)

The one Audi that held together all day was rapid, leading the midfield by a couple of tenths and picking off Isack Hadjar’s underperforming Red Bull for good measure. “The track was quite grippy today, FP2 especially, so quite in a happy place,” reported Gabriel Bortoleto. “I think the car was behaving well, I was driving well today.”

The key of course will be building on that encouraging start through Saturday, when conditions could change, and ensuring the car holds together well enough to avoid another scoring opportunity slipping through Audi’s fingers.

“Honestly, my car has been working OK this weekend, and hopefully it can keep up like this,” Bortoleto added, “and hopefully they fix also Nico's car, because we had a good performance this weekend, I'm sure he can come strong as well.” -

Loser: Nico Hulkenberg's Audi...

There was a bad case of deja vu for Audi where one side of the garage was again beset by reliability trouble.

In Mexico, Bortoleto logged no laps in FP1. In Brazil, it was Nico Hulkenberg’s turn – except he went one ‘better’, completing zero laps at all, all day.

That’s because FP1 stand-in Freddie Slater took over Hulkenberg’s car in the opening session, but ground to a halt with what eventually turned out to be a gearbox problem.

Not only did this ruin Slater’s outing one week after his Mexico FP1 debut was slightly limited by a different problem, it was so complicated to trace that by the time Audi had a handle on the issue it was too late to get everything ready for Hulkenberg to drive in FP2.

Racing director Allan McNish couldn’t hide his frustration. The only silver lining was the seven laps Slater did, he enjoyed, and the team was impressed by, as the 18-year-old has made a good impact with his approach off-track and the quality of the work he’s started to do on it. -

Winner: Haas (10th & 16th)

Ollie Bearman was within two tenths of the lead of the midfield in practice two on Friday, a welcome distraction from Haas's dramatic off-track headline-making with Rafael Camara replacing Esteban Ocon this weekend. The usual practice caveats apply but 10th is a very handy place for Haas to end its day, although its lack of pace on the hard tyre and the reprimand Camara received for badly impeding Leclerc means this entry has its drawbacks.

But quick on the softs, and with Camara doing "brilliantly" on his first day in the car, there's a silver lining to what was always going to be a tough weekend amid the current turmoil at this team. -

title: Doctors pull knife from man's eye that went through his brain—and he's fine now
author: Beth Mole
text:
A man in his 20s showed up to a UK hospital with the hilt of a knife sticking out of his face. The 15 mm-wide blade hidden within went completely through his right eye and through his brain, with the tip of the blade hitting the top of his skull.

Despite the ghastly injury, the man was alive and conscious when he arrived. He could still talk and move all four limbs. His doctors described him as being in a state of agitation. On the Glasgow Coma Scale, he scored a 12 (E3 V4 M5) , indicating a "moderate" brain injury, just one point above "mild." He could open his left eye when told, but otherwise kept it closed (E3 score); he could talk and answer questions, but was confused (V4); and he intentionally moved away when pressure was applied to his body (M5).

In a report published Friday in BMJ Case Report, his doctors said they were concerned that in his confused, agitated state he may try to pull the knife out on his own. So, they swiftly sedated and intubated him. They put him on prophylactic treatments for bacterial infections, including tetanus. Then they used images to see what was going on in his head.

title: Premier League news: Arteta insists Rice isn’t playing too many games
author: Guardian sport
text:
Carrick says it is possible to restore former glory at Old Trafford with time and Unai Emery confirms Aston Villa contract talks

Arteta agreed Rice had strengthened his ball progression, and explained his thinking behind dropping the 27-year-old deeper. “We cannot restrict his qualities and his capacities,” Arteta said. “He can drop back, he can progress play. He can drop back, he can carry the ball, he can be incredible in transition.

“He can win duels. He can produce passes by arriving, by playing far, by crossing the ball left or right, it doesn’t matter. On set pieces [too], he’s got a lot to offer. His shooting ability from long range as well is something that we need to use more.” PA

Unai Emery has confirmed he has held talks over signing a new contract with a view to building a “stronger” project at Aston Villa.

On Wednesday, the day after Villa’s 3-0 Champions League defeat at Barcelona, the club said they had held a meeting to discuss their long-term strategy beyond 2029, when Emery’s deal is due to expire.

The manager been linked with several clubs, including Manchester United, but was involved with long-term talks, including with the chair, Nassef Sawiris.

Emery said: “My ambition is to keep our consistency and how we are improving and building lots of things positively. It is a huge challenge. They decided, speaking with us last year, to build a new stand to add more supporters at Villa Park. That is a clear step forward to get better.

“How we are increasing our budget each year, and revenue through our performance by playing in Europe and improving players, selling players, then buying young talented players, this is the process and ambition we should keep in the future.

“I had a good meeting with Nassef Sawiris, very good meeting, very positive. Let’s talk next week, trying to get everything we spoke about together. We were speaking about how we can set our project stronger with a deal, yes.” PA

title: When a single vowel stands in the path to victory, the stakes could not be higher for these spelling bee champions
author: Caitlin Cassidy
text:
Primary school students bested 200,000 competitors across New South Wales to reach the Premier’s Spelling Bee finals in Sydney

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

Competing in a spelling bee is not for the faint of heart. Sometimes, the difference between victory and loss is one incorrect vowel and you’re undone, months of training reduced to nought.

At a small theatre hall in Sydney’s west on Friday afternoon, 34 primary school students sit stony-faced on a brightly lit stage, knowing this pressure only too well.

All have made it past about 200,000 students who competed in spelling bees across 1,070 public schools in New South Wales . The finalists earned their place at this year’s state competition after winning online regional finals in August. They represent the top 0.03%. And they’re not here to mess around.

Five are competing for a third time, having progressed to the last stage in the junior competition . Among them are year 5 student Wafiq Ayyash from the Hunter region, who won the junior state title in 2024, and year 6 student Bobby Ivaneza from the inner west, who was runner-up the same year.

Ewan Mattick from the state’s central west, Caleb Borg from the Riverina, and Alesha Kahfandi from the Hunter have also qualified for the state finals on three occasions. This isn’t their first rodeo.

The format is relatively simple. Contestants begin with “seen” words that they’ve been able to practise at home, before facing “unseen” words testing their broader skills and composure. Each round is sudden death.

To kick off, they’re introduced to the crowd by the host, ABC presenter Rae Johnston, with colourful details.

Archie Griffith likes the Parramatta Eels and his dachshund puppy. He doesn’t like his dad’s jokes. Ivaneza, who is wearing a bright red sweatband, admires Nicola Tesla, a Serbian-American engineer who died in 1943, for his genius. Ivaneza’s favourite food is camembert.

The students are as diverse as the schools they come from. Some 23 speak a language other than English at home, and 18 have travelled from outside Sydney.

Seven go down in the first round, stumbling over obscure words like “tourmaline” and “malapropism”. Another seven are out in round two – but you try spelling “lepidopterist” at home.

In the next four rounds, 13 students fall. Mattick nails “centurion” and gives a thumbs up to his family. Come round seven, Kahfandi begins to pray.

“Pernicious” and “sagacious” bring two more students down. And then there are five: Afeef Ahmed, Ivaneza, Kahfandi, Caroline Wang, and Maximilian Lumley, all in year 6. Two are returning finalists.

In round eight, they all spell their words correctly, though Ivaneza, usually breezing through with confidence, restarts on “whimsical”. Then, in round nine, he’s asked to spell “unserviceable” and omits the second “e”.

Ivaneza, visibly devastated, slumps into his seat and places his head in his hands. The remaining students spell their words correctly, and Ivaneza tearily returns to his family in the crowd and the comforting embrace of his father. The heartbreak is palpable.

Then, in an instant, after Ahmed correctly spells “immemorial”, the remaining three competitors fall. Kahfandi misses “antepenultimate”, Wang gets tied up by “parmigiana” and Lumley is one letter off getting “genealogy”. Ahmed has won.

“We are in an interesting situation,” Johnston says. “We need to play for a runner up.” Wang goes out straight away after being dealt the word “grandiloquent”. But Kahfandi and Lumley appear to be in lockstep. For the next five rounds, they’re either both correct or both wrong.

“We’re just going to keep on going,” Johnston declares. It begins to feel that the audience will grow old in this theatre, steadily working its way through the entire Macquarie Dictionary.

But then, Kahfandi misses the word “vociferous”. Lumley approaches the microphone and awaits his fate. His word is “apocalypse” and, after a deep breath, he nails it.

The crowd bursts into cheers, and Lumley returns to his seat and stares reflectively at the ground, looking like he has endured a war. His grandmother, Sue, is bursting with pride. “It was so stressful,” she says, “and he looked so calm.”

“He’s worked so hard. Some of those words, I didn’t even know what they were. We’re very proud.”

Kahfandi is proud of herself, too. “It was very tense in the room, there was a lot of pressure on everyone,” she says. “I feel a bit disappointed I didn’t get second and I was a bit tired after all those rounds, but getting third place is also really good.”

Ahmed is surprised he’s won, but his mother isn’t. She’s been helping him train for months – half an hour every night before bed.

“He reads a lot,” she says. “I knew he would win; he was three-time champion at school.”

Asked how he felt when he found out he’d won Ahmed says, at first, he “didn’t realise”.

“But then when they said we had a winner, I felt happy,” he says. “The runners-up words were harder than the ones I got.”

title: China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang
author: Jay Peters
text:
Nvidia’s CEO is reportedly the target of a ‘Chinese spy plot’ for intelligence on American AI chips.

Nvidia’s CEO is reportedly the target of a ‘Chinese spy plot’ for intelligence on American AI chips.

China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times . The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says.

Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new.

The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang , was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

title: Ultra-Wide and Coming in 29, 30.5, and 32 Sizes: The Newmen Streem G.48 CS
author: Josh Ross
text:
Today, German wheel brand Newmen has launched the Streem G.48 CS, a carbon wheelset that supersizes the modern gravel rim. If you aren’t familiar with Newmen, the company was founded in 2016 by former Syntace engineers Michi Grätz and Fabian Merz. They hit the market fast, presenting the very first products—the super-lightweight Advanced SL X.22 carbon wheelset and an aluminum sibling, the Evolution SL X.A.25—at the 2016 Eurobike show for the 2017 season. Since then, the brand has become known for designing lightweight, highly engineered cycling components—primarily wheelsets and cockpits. Most recently in the gravel world, though, it’s been ultra-wide wheels.

The latest Newmen Streem G.48 continues that thread with a 48mm deep carbon wheelset the brand positions as a “true all-rounder” covering everything from “after-work rides, bikepacking adventures or the next gravel race.”

As expected, this is a 48mm deep wheel, but what stands out is the width. The wheelset is built around a generous 45mm external width and a 27mm inner width that Newmen states is “perfectly matched to modern gravel tyres.” To manage handling and compliance, the brand uses a “bulbous rim profile” designed to “absorb impacts efficiently” while retaining an “extremely low sensitivity to crosswinds.” The rim uses a hooked tubeless-ready bead and hides the valve inside the rim using an internal aero valve system.

At the top of the range, the Streem G.48 CS model utilizes silver decals and features a claimed weight of 1,390 grams for the set. The CS build is laced with 21 VONOA Aero Wide Carbon spokes front and rear, attached to Newmen’s FADE R CS centerlock hubs. The hubs feature standard 12x100mm and 12x142mm spacing, support XD, Shimano HG, and Microspline freehub bodies, and are rated for 60Nm of max torque. The total max system weight for the wheelset is 130 kg.

All carbon-spoke wheelsets in the lineup are hand-built at the company’s facility in Kempten, Germany, while a forthcoming steel-spoke variant will be hand-built in the Czech Republic. Perhaps the biggest attention grabber in the news, though, is the detail that Newmen plans to offer more wheel sizes. As reported by BikeRadar, 30.5- and 32-inch diameter wheels will be available “in the future.”

Neither version of the Newmen Streem G.48 is currently available. The carbon-spoked version will eventually cost £1,499 and will be available first with the steel-spoked wheelset priced at £1,250 and promised starting in spring 2027. For more information visit the Newmen website .

title: Starlink Mobile: All the news on SpaceX’s major mobile carrier ambitions
author: Emma Roth
text:
SpaceX has declared that it’s going to make Starlink Mobile a “major” mobile carrier. The Elon Musk-owned company has already deployed thousands of direct-to-cell satellites, but its next big challenge is building out its 5G network here on Earth.

As part of its plans to rival AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, SpaceX has inked a deal with Qualcomm , which will deploy its cellular technology across tens of thousands of 5G cell sites starting in 2027. SpaceX is also reportedly in talks to buy Boost Mobile , potentially allowing it to launch Starlink Mobile through the service. Another report suggests SpaceX may tap into 80,000 cell sites across the US to build out its network.

SpaceX’s big plans have garnered some reactions in the telecom industry. Tim Höttges, the CEO of T-Mobile’s parent company Deutsche Telekom, said he takes SpaceX’s plans “super serious” but that it could cost Musk more than $200 billion to pull off.

Follow along for the latest updates on Starlink’s major mobile carrier ambitions.

Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier.

Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band spectrum to expand the Starlink network, spectrum that’s been traded around the telecom business for decades now. SpaceX’s ambitious plan is to use that spectrum to help build “the world’s most advanced mobile network.”

Bloomberg has a breakdown of how Starlink Mobile will operate — and what SpaceX still needs to do to get its hybrid 5G network up and running.

SpaceX is teaming up with Qualcomm to build out its nationwide mobile network. Under the multi-year deal, SpaceX will bring Qualcomm’s Dragonwing technology to “tens of thousands” of 5G cell sites across the US, with the first deployments set for 2027.

The news of the partnership comes as part of SpaceX’s push to make Starlink Mobile a “major” carrier in the US , competing directly with T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon. The Elon Musk-owned company has already snapped up a swath of spectrum , while recent reports suggested that SpaceX was exploring an acquisition of Boost Mobile .

SpaceX has discussed a deal with Boost Mobile to launch its own service through the budget-friendly carrier, according to a report from The Washington Post . The deal, which comes as SpaceX aims to make Starlink a “major” mobile carrier , reportedly involves the Elon Musk-owned company acquiring Boost Mobile or accessing its network.

Musk discussed the potential agreement with Charlie Ergen, chairman of Boost Mobile parent company EchoStar, last month, as reported by The Washington Post . Boost Mobile’s network is currently powered by T-Mobile and AT&T, meaning SpaceX may need permission from the two carriers to launch its service.

SpaceX plans to access at least 80,000 cell sites as part of efforts to compete directly with Verizon, T-Mobile, and AT&T, according to a report from Bloomberg . Sources tell the publication that SpaceX is in talks with Crown Castle Inc., one of the nation’s largest cell tower owners.

The move would give SpaceX access to half of the 158,500 cell towers currently operational in the US, according to Reuters . When asked about a potential partnership with SpaceX, Amazon, or other satellite services during an earnings call on Wednesday , Crown Castle CEO Chris Hillabrant said, “I don’t think I want to get into customer-specific detail, but you can assume that we’re talking to all parties.” SpaceX plans to pair a network of cell towers with its constellation of direct-to-cell satellites.

SpaceX has acquired a portfolio of low-band spectrum licenses — a move the company says “will pave the way” for its Starlink Mobile service to become a “major” US carrier. When the Federal Communications Commission signs off on the deal, SpaceX says it will deploy its new architecture that combines its satellite-to-mobile constellation with a terrestrial mobile network, directly competing with T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon.

The licenses include up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band, which SpaceX says will allow Starlink Mobile’s signal to penetrate through walls and buildings. SpaceX previously acquired 2GHz spectrum from EchoStar as part of efforts to bolster its direct-to-device service.

SpaceX is preparing to build a terrestrial mobile network to “acquire quite a few” of the customers now subscribed to T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon. The message to compete head-to-head with the US carriers was delivered by SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell and CEO Elon Musk during the Q&A section of the company’s first earnings call.

“The spectrum that we purchased from EchoStar does have terrestrial components, so we definitely intend to build out the terrestrial component,” said Shotwell. “You will have not only the capacity from the satellites themselves, but you will have a buildout of the terrestrial, basically the hardware and systems necessary to make a true mobile service exactly what you want it to be.”

title: Ships loiter near subsea cables amid Iran's warnings to Trump
author: Jeremy Hsu
text:
Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been loitering over subsea Internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz—a possible indication that the Iranian government is preparing to attack such undersea infrastructure in response to any renewed US and Israeli strikes.

The movements of three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat have been tracked near major undersea cables by the maritime intelligence firm Windward in October, according to the Financial Times . Six active cables currently cross through the contested Strait of Hormuz, linking the Middle East to Europe, Africa and Asia, with two more cables having segments under construction in the region.

Four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, depend entirely upon such subsea telecommunications connections running through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint to link with the outside world. But other countries also depend heavily on the region's undersea cable network—one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.

title: ‘Dangerous’ but also ‘brilliant’ - Rafael Camara’s F1 debut
author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
text:
New Haas driver Rafa Camara received a reprimand on his Formula 1 debut for what was deemed “clearly dangerous” impeding of Charles Leclerc in Brazilian Grand Prix practice.

Camara weaved and moved into the racing line as he prepared to start a push lap in FP2 at Interlagos just as Leclerc was coming by to complete a lap of his own.

Though he was warned several times that Leclerc was approaching, Camara ended up squeezing the Ferrari towards the run-off at high speed “with a significantamount of the car off the track”, said the stewards, who upgraded the typical practice penalty for impeding from a warning to a formal reprimand.

“The situation that was created was clearly dangerous and [Camara] should have taken more care to avoid impeding [Leclerc]."

Camara’s incident with Leclerc was a blot on an otherwise solid and steadily improving first day in the car.

He finished 0.86s slower than Ollie Bearman in FP1, and trimmed the gap to 0.57s in FP2, with the biggest part of his time lost in the middle sector - although he had been even closer on the initial hard-tyre push laps before switching to softs.

There was a recurring problem under braking into Turn 1, where Camara had huge run-ending lock-ups in both FP1 and FP2, although several drivers had trouble here.

And he was still trying to smoothen his throttle usage exiting Turns 2 and 12 by the end of Friday as well.

But considering Camara has been thrown in at the deep end with a lot of procedural stuff to learn as well as getting on top of a 2026 car he is driving for the first time, Haas felt he had a “pretty strong day”, head of car engineering Hoagy Nidd said.

“Obviously a massive learning curve today, it's pretty intimidating, but he did brilliantly,” said Nidd.

“He built up steadily through FP1. He was sort of almost a bit reticent to give too much feedback from FP1 and obviously for FP2 he was improving all the time and building with his feedback and his driving, so a pretty strong day I would say.

“Working on procedures, you probably saw us go out, do a few starts, things like that, just the normal bread and butter things that we almost take for granted with most drivers, so we're very pleased with him I think.”

title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
text:
Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.

He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.

But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."

With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.

Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it " the best vehicle Tesla has ever made , external " as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".

Musk responded to the user , external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."

The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was " way more awesome than people realise , external " in March, and called it the " best product Tesla has ever made to date , external " in April.

But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.

It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.

Despite the gaffe, the Cybertruck ended up receiving a 146,000 orders, Musk said in 2019 , while it was still in development.

In the end, the vehicle launched in 2023, keeping its novel design - an angular shape with a body made of stainless steel.

Tesla fans praised its retro-futuristic look, which some said looked like something " straight out of Blade Runner , external ".

But critics were far less kind, joking about its appearance and labelling it " ugly as sin , external ".

Several recalls - including in 2025 affecting more than 46,000 Cybertrucks over concerns part of its trim could fall off - would not have helped.

"We need to make it at a price that people can afford," Musk told Wall Street analysts that year - which ended up being $61,000 (then £48,000) for all the "bells and whistles".

In 2026, the so-called "Cyberbeast" model comes in at $102,000.

title: Mariners hire Tanner Swanson away from Yankees
author: Madison Pavich
text:
Another key member of the supporting cast of coaches has left town.

For the second time this week, the Yankees have lost a significant member of their coaching staff. Tanner Swanson, the organization’s director of catching since 2020, has been hired by the Seattle Mariners to join new manager Jason Kanzler as their bench coach according to the New York Post’s Joel Sherman . This comes on the heels of Triple-A manager Shelley Duncan defecting over to the Red Sox on Wednesday to join their staff, and now despite not making any firings of their own on the coaching staff the Yankees will have some holes to fill.

Swanson was revolutionary in the organization for developing the team’s ability to frame pitches. Austin Wells has become the model for his work, becoming one of the best pitch framers in the game, and his development lined up directly with Swanson’s arrival in New York. The Yankees have been providing catchers to several teams over the years though, as they traded from their surplus of catchers sending Carlos Narváez over to Boston for Elmer Rodriguez, flipping Jose Trevino to Cincinnati for Fernando Cruz, and including Kyle Higashioka in the package to San Diego that netted Juan Soto.

The loss of Swanson is a big one for the Yankees to swallow, but they’ve hopefully learned enough from his time here to continue the catching pipeline that has netted them so much value. For Swanson, the chance to coach in the major leagues is an opportunity that he couldn’t pass up on, and he’ll now get to work with a premier catcher in Cal Raleigh coming off what was a disappointing follow-up to his MVP runner-up 2025.

title: Yankees Mailbag: An early look at outfield options
author: Madison Pavich
text:
The Yankees could use an outfielder if they want to have the best unit in baseball, but is there a clean fit?

Good afternoon everyone, it’s time to dive back into the mailbag and answer some of your questions. Remember to send in your questions for our bi-weekly call by e-mail to pinstripealleyblog [at] gmail [dot] com .

Darth_Lazarus asks: If the CBA negotiations go really sideways is there a possibility we see replacement player games next year?

Never say never, but I doubt the owners would want to go this route even if it’s looking like the season is completely lost. Recruiting scab players at this point in the league’s history would be a black eye on ownership and would completely kill any goodwill they could have with the public as these negotiations drag on, as the product on the field will be a clearly inferior copy that wouldn’t draw much interest while also making them look desperate to recoup on the broadcast deals they’ve negotiated. Speaking of those broadcasting rights, while the league is a much more regional product than the NFL or NBA and several teams were having trouble finding an actual partner for their TV audience, it’s my hope that the prospect of future negotiations with broadcasters is one of the pressure points pushing ownership to get to the table sooner rather than later resulting in an actual season being played out in 2027 — perhaps a bit too hopeful, considering the lines in the sand that have been drawn this time around, but a girl can dream.

LocalBlueWhaleRuinsEverything asks: With the Yankees needing some offense, could they consider Arozarena or Suzuki? Theoretically, they could stick one in LF and have Cody move to CF. It’s not something I’d want them to do long term, but for one season I’d be interested. Stanton and Garcia should be gone after next season, so in the future you’d a spare DH spot to rotate them.

Theoretically they could, but that takes a lot of the value that Bellinger provides away by moving his excellent left field defense over to center field, where he has been underwhelming at best since 2021. Arozarena and Suzuki are both quality offensive options that would improve the lineup tremendously, but the defensive setback that adding either would cause problems down the line. That being said, the free agent market for true center fielders is abysmal, so if they’re looking for an upgrade they’re going to have to get creative with trades to find it.

Johnny1944 asks: It seems JD was overhyped for years by Cash. Does he have any real value?

Jasson Domínguez’s career is looking like a relatively unremarkable one, which is what tends to happen to the majority of MLB players — but most players don’t get compared to Mickey Mantle when they were 17 years old. That unfair expectation has felt like a weight on Domínguez’s shoulders the entire time that he’s been in the organization, with every glimpse of a solid run down in the minors being heralded as the turning point where he was going to spark a path straight to the majors. However, Domínguez has now had two full seasons in proximity to the majors, and while he’s still very young entering his age-24 season in 2027 it just doesn’t seem like there’s much to work with in his game.

Our own Andrés tackled the idea of whether the Yankees should move on from Domínguez the other day, and while his conclusion was that there’s no pressure to do so immediately time is running out for the former wonder prospect. He’s got one minor league option remaining meaning he’s likely to start the year in the minors, and while there’s some underlying promise in his peripherals the majority of his Savant page is disappointing. Domínguez’s defense has been atrocious to watch, and he’s alternated from being unable to hit lefties to being unable to hit righties. If there was just some consistency to his game he’d at least be able to stick around as a bench option in the majors, but as is he’s got to get consistent playing time to try and make something of himself and he isn’t going to find that in pinstripes at the moment.

OLDY MOLDY asks: How reliable are Cole, Fried, and Rodón next year considering recent arm problems in the last 3 seasons and age? Any innings projections? Does Schlittler come back to earth in 2027?

I don’t have many concerns about Max Fried at the moment — he’ll probably be good for one short-term IL stint but otherwise give the team 25-30 starts and has been lights out when he has been active. Likewise, while Gerrit Cole has missed significant time over the past couple of seasons the core issue has now been dealt with and he should be fully healthy entering 2027. It’s wild to think that we’re already seven years into the nine-year deal that Cole signed with the team, but there’s just two seasons left of his contract and if you told me back then that he’d have compiled three top five Cy Young finishes with one win up to this point, I’d be pretty content entering the final days of that deal. Carlos Rodón has salvaged his Yankees career quite well following his disastrous first year in pinstripes, but of the three his health still concerns me more going forward — not enough to panic, but enough to keep my eye on how he’s getting through each start even when he’s on. As for Cam Schlittler, the sky is the ceiling for the team’s newfound ace and while it would certainly be unrealistic to expect a 1.95 ERA as the standard going forward I think he’ll remain the team’s best pitcher next year as he comes into his own.

title: Global stocks fall amid ‘big worries over AI’ after Democrats’ midterms triumph
author: Mark Sweney and Graeme Wearden
text:
Asian and European markets follow Wall Street with sharp fall as FTSE down 1.9%

European stock markets have fallen sharply as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fears of a slowdown in the AI industry.

A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stocks markets on Friday morning. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market is poised for its worst day since March.

The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down 207 points, or 1.9%, at 10,575 points in mid-morning trading.

Germany’s Dax index fell by 1.9% in morning trading, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 1.5% and Spain’s Ibex lost 1.1%.

Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe .

“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”

On Thursday the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.

Chip stocks led the slump, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by 61% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.

The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 8%.

“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets. “[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come.

“Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.”

However, despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year.

The Nasdaq Composite index remains up 4.6% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.

The FTSE 100 has gained almost 6.9% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.

Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said that while he did not expect a quick rebound from Thursday’s losses in the US, he also did not believe it marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade”.

He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.”

Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper set for its biggest weekly fall since March.

Benchmark three-month copper, a key metal used in the semiconductor, electronics and automotive industry, has dropped 0.61%, leaving it positioned for a 2.79% fall this week.

Craig Lang, a principal analyst at the consultancy CRU, said the price of copper was increasingly influenced by the AI market and “sentiment towards datacentre expansion”.

title: Three men charged in US with using AI to impersonate CEOs and steal millions
author: Johana Bhuiyan
text:
Men allegedly impersonated voices and images of executives to convince employees to send large payments

Three foreign nationals were arrested and charged with using AI to allegedly impersonate corporate CEOs and attorneys to steal over $100m, according to an indictment that was newly unsealed by the US Department of Justice.

According to a press release from the United States attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, three men – Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit – were arrested for using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys at various companies in order to convince employees to send over large payments. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain over the summer, while Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. The alleged fraud took place between 2024 and 2026.

With the help of AI, the men allegedly acted as a corporate executive, targeting employees of various companies and telling them they needed their help with sensitive financial transactions. They would then instruct the employees to get in touch with lawyers at a large international law firm. The men would then impersonate a lawyer at these firms and have the employees wire a large amount of money.

The men ultimately stole more than $129m from companies all over the world including in the US, according to the DoJ. The men allegedly stole nearly $5m from a hospital system headquartered in Missouri; about $2.7m from a Rhode Island bank, about $3m from a California hospital system, over $4.6m from a mutual fund headquartered in Massachusetts and about $5m from a pet food company in Florida. The men also stole over $11m from a UK tech company.

The men would direct employees to wire money to bank accounts all over the world including in the United States, Spain , Portugal, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China. After the money had been wired, the men would covert the money into cryptocurrency “in an attempt to conceal the source, ownership, and control of the stolen proceeds and distributed it amongst themselves and their co-conspirators”, according to the DoJ press release. Soall and Hazan went by several aliases: Soal’s nicknames included “Seba Clarke” and “Rocky Balboa,” while Hazan went by “Superman Cash,” “Fat Boy,” and “Ron.”

In a statement, Jamie McDonald, a US attorney, said artificial intelligence had great potential but that the public should recognize that some may seek to use the technology to pursue criminal goals.

“The alleged scheme orchestrated by Soall, Hazan, and Sheetrit demonstrates how the use of advanced technology can be exploited to commit large-scale fraud,” said James C Barnacle Jr, the FBI assistant director in charge, in a statement. “As criminals continue to weaponize emerging technologies, the FBI remains committed to rapidly adapting our capabilities to identify, investigate, and disrupt those who seek to harm New Yorkers and businesses operating in our communities.”

The men have been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, various counts of money-laundering conspiracy and aggravated identity theft.

title: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
text:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have been climbing following an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index opened higher following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.

Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.

However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.

On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.

But the Nasdaq Composite opened up on Friday and flattened out around 1.7% higher by lunchtime, reversing some of its 5.5% fall.

The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, was around 0.9% higher by lunchtime. The Dow Jones Industrial Average opened a little down before nudging into positive territory.

Nvidia, which shed hundreds of billions in market value on Thursday after shares slid more than 9%, began Friday up more than 6% but settled around 4% higher as trading continued.

SpaceX and Tesla shares, which were also hammered on Thursday, saw more mixed gains, up more than 6% and nearly 5% respectively.

Chipmakers AMD and Micron both dropped by more than 17% on Thursday, but AMD shares had risen by about 12% on Friday while Micron was up more than 8%.

However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse on Friday.

The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.

In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.

In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.

"While no-one knows what happens next, it's clear that we've just seen a significant shift in market sentiment," he said.

"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?

Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck

The market fluctuations come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.

A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.

US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".

However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.

Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.

"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.

"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."

He said people were watching firms come into their communities and build data centres while their own energy costs were going up, and those companies "have to be better neighbours".

As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.

And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.

Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.

Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.

"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

We regret to inform you...

Last Friday, Chainalysis said it had been the target of a cybersecurity incident in October that was similar to the hacks of other platforms during the same month. title: Ferrari's Hamilton-Leclerc problem - and other F1 stories to follow
text:
The drivers' title is sewn up, and the constructors' may well be on Sunday, but Formula 1 marches restlessly, relentlessly on.

This weekend's Sao Paulo Grand Prix is in many ways the first page of the first chapter of the next championship battle.

New world champion Kimi Antonelli says he sees the final races of the season as preparation to defend his title in 2027, and his vanquished Mercedes team-mate George Russell is working on understanding where things went wrong, with the aim of putting them right.

The team's main target this weekend is securing the three points more than Ferrari they need to lock away the constructors' championship, to underline their return to the form they showed for so long in the 2010s.

Mercedes' rivals, meanwhile, are continuing the work that has seen them turn what was a chasm in performance at the beginning of the year into a highly competitive battle between the top four teams at the end.

The season has been in two parts. Mercedes dominated the first third, winning seven of the first eight races.

Since then, Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull have all had their time in the sun, and out of the past 12 races, Mercedes have won six, Red Bull three, McLaren two and Ferrari one.

Only the beginnings of a competitive picture have emerged in Sao Paulo, with Antonelli and Lando Norris in an upgraded McLaren initially appearing in good shape in Friday practice, but beyond that there are a number of running narratives to maintain the interest.

Chief among them is the tension between Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc after they contrived to throw away a potential one-two finish in Mexico last Sunday by tangling on the first lap.

After that race, Hamilton said the team had "big problems" and needed "serious talks".

Those happened on Thursday evening, after Leclerc and team principal Frederic Vasseur arrived back in Brazil having returned to Europe between races.

Vasseur said on Friday: "It went well. It was good to discuss. It was good to clarify our positions and now we turn the page.

"The guidelines are still the same. They need to respect each other. They are competitive with fighting spirit but they need to respect the other one and the brand and the people working back home and on track.

"The message was clear and will stay clear. Overall it is true that they are working for the team and the team has to come first. It's clear we failed and we have to react but the meeting was a clear reminder that Ferrari comes first."

The magnitude of this situation is obvious, as is the difficulty in finding a solution, and the potential for further trouble down the line.

Hamilton has been especially outspoken on this topic.

The seven-time champion has drawn a contrast between the way Leclerc races him and the way he approaches other drivers, pointing to him ceding to Max Verstappen when they were racing side by side to the first corner in Singapore, compared with how he dealt with Hamilton in Mexico City.

"We could have easily had a one-two and so we definitely have to work towards making sure that doesn't happen again," Hamilton said, adding that he thought this was a theme between Leclerc and his team-mates that he had also seen with his predecessors Sebastian Vettel and Carlos Sainz.

He also said: "Of course, there's some times you say things and maybe you might regret it afterwards, but I don't.

"I've never apologised for being authentic and real. And I'm not going to be silenced. I have not been asked to not say anything. And that's just the way it is.

"I wear my heart on my sleeve and I say how I feel in the moment."

From Vasseur's point of view, this is a problem that really needs to be solved because if Ferrari can keep hold of the chassis advantage they have had this year and bring their engine up to the level of Mercedes and Red Bull, they could be title contenders next year.

Hamilton said: "Naturally, it's not so easy having someone like me come into a team because I'm very outspoken and I push and push and push, push for so many changes and I'm going to be pushing for more.

"As long as I'm here, that's how it's going to be. I'm here to win. And to be able to win, you have to work with everyone around you.

"I truly believe that this team can be fighting for the championship next year.

"I'm in the process of working with the head of aero, the head of aerodynamics to make sure that we hold on to the goodness of the car we have this year and fix some of the small, subtle things that could be better.

"And obviously, the power-unit, they're doing their thing and I really hope that they're able to pull through."

At Red Bull, the situation is much simpler as the team build serious momentum in this final part of the season.

Verstappen was the beneficiary of the Ferrari battle in Mexico, and his victory there was his third in four races.

That has moved him up into second in the drivers' championship - something that looked impossible as the team floundered in the first third of the year, when they were not far off a second off the pace.

"It's a big surprise to be second in the championship, but we take it," Verstappen said.

"We had a lot of difficulties as a team in the beginning. The car was not where we wanted it to be. Probably also we still had to learn quite a bit from the power units, and I think we really learned a lot throughout the season.

"From my side, it's just you never really give up or, in terms of, like, you just never really settle for P6 or P7, right?

"Even when I was in that position or fighting the midfield, I was still trying to do the best that I could get out of the situation.

"Sometimes that is a P6 when the car is not able to perform better. But then once the car is in a better window, then you can fight further up front and eventually, of course, win races.…

title: Earth's churning mantle may have created the Great Unconformity
author: Jacek Krywko
text:
In the Grand Canyon, there is a line in the rock where time seems to have gone missing. Ancient crystalline rocks mark its bottom, while sandstones laid down as life started to diversify during the Cambrian explosion mark the top. “It’s called the Great Unconformity, and it’s a gap in the geologic record,” says Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong, Australia. "This gap can be anywhere between 200 million years, which is not that impressive, to more than a billion years.”

In a recent Nature study, Flament and his colleague Santosh Dhungana argue that this gap was carved with help from deep within the planet. According to their models, slow currents of hot rock in Earth's mantle pushed entire continents up for hundreds of millions of years, letting glaciers grind them down and then let them sink, allowing fresh sediments to bury the scar. The largest hole in the rock record might be a fingerprint of processes happening deep in the planet's interior.

The oldest sediments resting on the Great Unconformity in North America are between 635 and 482 million years old. Geologists have traced it across most of North America and parts of northern Europe and northern China. “Something seems to have happened, in particular in North America,” Flament says.

title: Wolff backs MotoGP's handling of calendar dissent
author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
text:
Mercedes Formula 1 boss Toto Wolff has backed MotoGP's handling of its Qatar Grand Prix amid rider discontent, ahead of F1's own planned races in the region.

While F1 has gathered at Interlagos for the Brazilian Grand Prix, MotoGP is competing at Qatar's Lusail circuit on the same weekend - with 16 of the 22 full-time riders (and two injury replacements) in action.

This followed several secret and unofficial votes between the MotoGP riders, in which the majority had voted against holding a Qatar race due to fears of conflict escalation in the Middle East.

In the end, though, only the Yamaha riders - those representing the factory team and the satellite team Pramac - are absent from the Qatar GP without replacement.

Yamaha announced last Sunday that it "had not identified sufficient grounds to change its existing company-wide travel restrictions" to send its teams to Qatar, a decision that was met with "disappointment" and suggestion of "sporting consequences" from MotoGP.

The series emphasised it did not "receive any information that would warrant a change to the current plans for the event" after consultation with Qatar, the track and "independent safety advisors".

As for the riders present in Qatar, some have taken a more conciliatory stance over the handling of the event, but others have maintained a more confrontational tone.

Notably, seven-time series champion Marc Marquez said in the pre-event press conference: "I would like to be in another place. For that reason I arrive on the latest flight possible, and I will leave on the earliest flight possible."

F1 has two races scheduled in the region - November 29's Qatar GP, and December 6's Abu Dhabi GP.

And when asked at Interlagos whether his understanding of the situation with those races was being informed with MotoGP racing at Qatar this weekend, Wolff offered an extensive answer that backed MotoGP's approach and questioned what the riders have shared publicly.

"Stefano [Domenicali, F1 boss] and Mohammed [Ben Sulayem, FIA president] have been pretty clear about the situation, that Formula 1 follows what the international guidelines are, whether there's travel restrictions, airlines not flying, any warnings in the region, the kind of feedback that local governments are making - so not only the promoters, but what the local governments are making. And this is what you need to rely on, in my opinion," Wolff said.

"And I'm fully with that. I think that if riders stand up, that geopolitically know nothing about what's going on but [they] have the audience that listens, I think that is something that creates media value [headlines] - but I would have done the same that MotoGP management has done.

"You want to ride, or drive, go. If you don't want to, don't go. As simple as that.

"And everybody can take their personal decisions on that, and I respect it. Of course, you've got to be wary of what's happening in the next few days, or few weeks.

"And Stefano has the finger on the pulse to monitor that. If things were to get more dangerous, then he's going to be the first one, together with Mohammed, to protect the people that were meant to travel. And so that's why I'm following the guidance of what I'm hearing.

"Internally it hasn't been raised, hasn't been a topic. But also there, if someone feels he or she doesn't feel comfortable in travelling, then it's something that I would always respect.

"And maybe that's an opportunity to give somebody else a chance.

"It wouldn't change anything for the relationship. I've always respected that, that some people didn't want to go to certain grands prix. And that's how I see it at the moment."

Crunch time for F1 calendar

Wolff’s comments come ahead of a crunch week for Formula 1 when it comes to defining how the 2026 season will end.

For a while now, Imola has been getting its venue ready as a fallback option in case the final Middle Eastern races cannot happen.

However, it is now at the point where it needs to commit to the final major preparations or abandon its work because the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are happening.

It is understood that F1 has set itself a deadline of next Tuesday (November 10) to make a final call on what to do with the Imola event.

If by then it is satisfied that the Middle Eastern races are good to go, then Imola can be stood down.

That call means, however, that if after that date tensions escalate in the Middle East and the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi have to be halted, then it means Imola will not be able to host any more – which means the season would finish in Las Vegas.

While the situation in the Middle East remains unpredictable, F1 teams retain faith that no "risks" will be taken in the final call.

Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack said that despite team personnel asking more questions about what was happening, there was confidence in F1’s senior management.

Speaking on Thursday at Interlagos, Krack said: “Now, I discussed it at length with Andy [Stevenson, sporting director] this morning, and we think, we are really convinced, that F1 is not taking any unnecessary risk.

“They are aware of the situation, they have much better information than we have. And I think if there is a serious risk, I think they will take the correct action.

“I think at the moment they are still evaluating that situation, and I’m sure they have set themselves some deadlines, which we have not gone over yet. So, I think we need to give them the time to do that. But I would be really surprised if they take risks.”

title: What happened in F1 2026 Brazilian GP second practice
author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
text:
Kimi Antonelli showed no signs of becoming complacent after his recently-sealed 2026 Formula 1 title win as he completed his domination of Friday practice in Brazil.

Antonelli topped FP2 with a comfortable 0.253s margin ahead of McLaren’s Lando Norris, who headed a gaggle of other cars.

In fact, the gap the lead Mercedes had over a mixed-up cast of would-be contenders at Interlagos reflected how 2026 has tended to play out overall.

Norris, Max Verstappen's Red Bull and George Russell's Mercedes were covered by just 0.020s, while Oscar Piastri was fifth in the second McLaren only half a tenth further back.

Verstappen was once again displeased with some engine behaviour in this session - and his confusion over Red Bull’s slightly vague update on how it was "adapting" to him prompted an amusing radio exchange where Verstappen suggested he should start talking to the clutch directly.

Less funny was the fact he ended the session early in the garage as a steering issue emerged that Red Bull could not quickly resolve.

In performance terms, the outlier at the moment is Ferrari, which seems to be struggling on balance but also (as usual) with straightline speed.

Lewis Hamilton led the team in sixth, nearly three tenths ahead of Charles Leclerc – who survived a high-speed near-miss when F1 debutant Rafa Camara’s Haas inadvertently squeezed him coming onto the start-finish straight.

Camara, who ended his first day as an F1 driver 16th fastest and just over half a second slower than Haas team-mate Ollie Bearman, will be investigated after the session for the incident.

He was preparing to start a lap when he squeezed Leclerc, who was finishing one, towards the run-off as they navigated the flat-out kink of Turn 15.

Leclerc kept his foot in over the bumpy run-off and managed to finish the lap, losing a couple of tenths in the process, and expressed his irritation afterwards.

These were Leclerc’s first laps of the weekend after Dino Beganovic drove his car in FP1.

Early on Leclerc complained that the balance was too far to the rear, and at the end of the session he was asking about the engine.

Towards the foot of the top 10, Gabriel Bortoleto was eighth in his Audi on home soil, just over a second off Antonelli but ahead of Isack Hadjar's Red Bull.

Ollie Bearman's Haas completed the top 10 but there was just half a tenth covering him, Franco Colapinto's Alpine and the Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson.

The only driver not to set a time was Nico Hulkenberg, who did not run at all after the issue that stopped Freddie Slater on track in FP1 could not be addressed by Audi in time, leaving Hulkenberg without a single lap in the car on Friday.

For those who did drive, there was a recurring challenge for almost everybody: lock-ups into the first corner.

At least half the field had a big moment under braking for the Senna S, struggling with the bumps as the track falls away, which could be a precursor to a defining performance differentiator come qualifying on Saturday.

Nvidia hardware worth $11.4M vanished between Oakland and Texas
author: Nick Indge
text:
A shipment of Nvidia hardware valued at $11.4 million vanished in transport between Oakland and Texas over the summer, and more than two months later, police have announced no arrests or recovery of the cargo.

As reported by The Mercury News , six pallets of unknown Nvidia equipment left Oakland on August 29 on a truck bound for Fort Worth, Texas. The hardware was reportedly picked up as scheduled by a truck bearing the logo of a food transportation company before vanishing off the grid. The theft wasn't noticed until early September, when the buyers realized that the shipment had never been received. Police attempting to trace the truck's route found it had made several multi-hour stops after picking up the hardware before losing the truck somewhere in San Bernardino County, California.

Oakland police confirmed that there was a grand theft report filed on September 13 and that the investigation remains ongoing. Authorities have not said what Nvidia hardware was stolen or exactly how the theft was carried out.
