title: Anti-fire ant eradication activist convicted after using legal arguments ‘similar to sovereign citizens’
author: Andrew Messenger
text:
Legal expert compares Trevor Hold’s failed defence to ‘tried and tested argument’ used by sovereign citizen movement

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

The Queensland leader of a group opposing the eradication of fire ants in Australia has been convicted of obstructing government officers, after a magistrate threw out his argument that the commonwealth-funded program is illegal.

Trevor Hold was fined $1,500 but a conviction was not recorded. Hold has described himself as an “ultrapreneur”, a mental health counsellor, an organic cattle farmer and the chief executive officer of the anti-program group the Australian Advocacy Group – and as self-employed.

He was convicted last month of two counts of obstruction for attempting to prevent fire ant treatment at his property, in what is believed to be a Queensland first.

His organisation and others held a series of well attended meetings last year across south-east Queensland to advise residents on what the group called their legal rights to refuse or prevent access to their properties to the program.

Under Queensland’s Biosecurity Act, landholders must permit program officers to access their property to treat fire ants, which are a declared priority pest.

But the organisations advised landholders to use a provision in the act allowing them to obstruct an officer if they had a “reasonable excuse” to refuse access, a provision in the Biosecurity Act.

On 16 April at about 9.20am, Hold prevented officers from entering his property in Adare in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane . The property was in the treatment zone and due for its annual treatment.

The eradication program had informed Hold in advance that it would treat his property that day. A small group of supporters gathered to film and yell at them while they did so, according to court documents.

The scene was later described as “an increasingly rowdy and crowded and dynamic situation” in the Ipswich magistrates court, which heard Hold’s charges last month.

He was arrested by Queensland police after about 40 minutes for obstructing them by not allowing a gate to be opened. He was then un-arrested. Despite being warned again, he was again arrested after another interaction with program officers.

Hold made three arguments to the magistrate, Leanne Scoines, in his defence.

He argued that he was intimidated by the police and the program officers and “withdrew his consent for their attendance”, describing himself as “frazzled”.

“It was put to Mr Hold that he was not frazzled, and that he had said on three occasions, as heard in the body-worn camera footage, that ‘this is the Trevor Hold show’,” Scoines said.

Through his lawyer, solicitor Beatrice Ludwig, Hold argued that the police had failed to take into account his “reasonable excuse” and were therefore acting outside their powers.

Hold based part of his argument on emails he sent to the Department of Primary Industries in December 2024 and January 2025, notices the magistrate described as “unilateral”, “quasi-legal documents … seeking tacit approval by non-response”. The magistrate found they were of no legal effect.

Finally, he challenged the validity of the program, arguing that the prosecution had not proven it was properly authorised under the Biosecurity Act, Scoines said.

All three arguments were dismissed and the magistrate found that the officers were entitled to proceed on the basis that the DPI officers were exercising powers conferred on them by the Biosecurity Act.

“I am not satisfied that Mr Hold was a credible or liable witness on the critical issues in dispute,” she said.

A police prosecutor told the court “In my respectful submission it was clear he was actually enjoying this incident”.

Hold has appealed against the judgment to the district court.

On his website, Hold advertises fundraising efforts for his defence, and also a mooted class action lawsuit against the program.

Southern Cross University professor David Heilpern compared some of the arguments used by Hold to sovereign citizen cases he used to judge as a magistrate in the NSW Northern Rivers region, particularly his claim that he hadn’t consented to fire ant treatment.

“That is a tried and tested argument in terms of many of those who are on the fringe of or deep into the sovereign citizen movement ; that you have a right to remove consent from the operations of various laws,” Heilpern said.

“Whether you consent or don’t consent is completely immaterial under the biosecurity legislation.”

title: The Victorian Liberals’ campaign bus was supposed to be a reset. Instead it became the symbol of a rough week
author: Benita Kolovos
text:
Crashing into a shop awning ended the first outing of the Jess Express – but the opposition’s electoral momentum will be harder to stop

Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast

Jess Wilson has barely put a foot wrong since becoming Victorian Liberal leader a little under a year ago. That was until this week, which ended with her campaign bus reversing into a small business .

The bus was launched on Friday, a few days earlier than planned, in what appeared to be an effort to reset Wilson’s relationship with the Spring Street press pack.

A day earlier, journalists had been left waiting for an hour as Wilson announced a $100m investment in medical research to an enthusiastic room of researchers at the Burnet Institute. But when it came to questions she stayed for just four minutes and 39 seconds – answering a single question from each of the nine journalists present before cutting the press conference short.

The pack had been keen to press Wilson on Labor’s claim that the Coalition’s election policies would cost $6.35bn more than they had disclosed.

The treasurer, Colin Brooks, had earlier spent 20 minutes taking journalists through a glossy booklet Labor titled “Jess Wilson’s Dodgy Costings”, which detailed 30 Coalition promises it claimed had not been costed and dozens it said the opposition had underquoted.

It was an interesting stunt given Labor has its own cost blowouts and financial problems – including net debt that is forecast to reach $199bn within four years. But they are not the only ones questioning how the Coalition plans to deliver a surplus by 2032 while making $8bn worth of election promises, offering tax cuts and vowing not to cut frontline services.

The Liberals have made much of their credentials as better economic managers than Labor and Wilson, as shadow treasurer, should have been prepared to stay and defend her own numbers.

The moment played into Brooks’s suggestion earlier in the day that the Liberals “don’t want to be subject to the scrutiny of having journalists … asking questions during the day”.

“They’re thinking they’re going to coast home to this election result, and that’s treating the Victorian people with contempt,” he said.

A similar thing happened last week, when Wilson’s team cancelled a press conference amid confusion over the Coalition’s plan to “pause and review” the multibillion-dollar Suburban Rail Loop project.

Then there is the debate brouhaha. Both News24 and Nine had requested a debate involving Wilson, the Labor premier, Ben Carroll, and the One Nation leader, Warren Pickering – given the latter is now commanding about 20% of primary votes in most polls.

Wilson has refused, instead insisting on a traditional one-on-one format with Labor, arguing that only the two major parties could form government. Carrollwants Pickering to be included, seemingly keen to keep alive the idea of a Liberal-One Nation coalition despite polling suggesting the Liberal-National Coalition should be able to win government in its own right.

Last week, News24 seemed to resolve the impasse by also inviting the Greens leader, Ellen Sandell.

But no agreement has been reached on Nine’s proposal. Wilson issued a statement on Thursday saying she had agreed to debate Carroll next week. This time Labor refused, claiming Nine has offered Pickering the opportunity to appear in a separate 10-minute segment during the same broadcast.

The Liberals reset on Friday, unveiling the “Jess Express” campaign bus.

Wilson was joined by her team and recruits from Canberra – including her close friend and federal Liberal senator James Paterson, and Kane Silom, who has taken leave from his role as communications director for the federal Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, to work on the Victorian campaign.

She chatted with journalists on the bus before it arrived at a Bentleigh cafe, where she made coffees and served brunch before a press conference, this time clocking in at more than 20 minutes.

Pressed again on her party’s costings, she said voters would have to wait until after early voting begins to see them.

“We cannot release our costings until the government has released its pre-election budget update,” Wilson said.

She batted off questions about the Liberals’ latest election commitment – to sell $1.3bn worth of government-owned land. Labor says this is more “dodgy costings” as it includes land earmarked for first home buyers, and a plot where radioactive cow carcasses were buried that would cost millions to clean up.

“Those costs have been factored in as part of the independent costings by the Parliamentary Budget Office,” Wilson said.

Then it was back on the bus and to the Centre Road shops – one of which became the victim of the Jess Express.

But perhaps there’s a glimmer of hope. Despite the damage, the store owner wasn’t too fussed, provided his awning is repaired.

Nor was it enough for him to rule out voting Liberal – he said he was still undecided.

It will take a little more to stop the Coalition momentum at this stage of the campaign.

Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent

title: Fearing AI disruption, white-collar workers are quitting their jobs
author: Amelia Penniman
text:
While there’s no evidence linking AI to mass layoffs, the tech has already ‘changed worker psychology’

W hen artificial intelligence researcher Mrinank Sharma quit his job at Anthropic earlier this year, the news rippled across the internet. In his resignation letter, posted on X and viewed 15.3m times, Sharma warned of a world “in peril” from the technology he had helped build.

“It is clear to me the time has come to move on,” he wrote. His next move: a poetry degree.

In the months following Sharma’s resignation, AI industry defectors and workers outside of Silicon Valley alike have echoed his sentiments.

Bracing for disruption forecasted by the AI industry, white-collar professionals are voluntarily leaving established careers to pursue professions they feel are more secure or more aligned with their values. Workers across industries – from tech to public relations to consulting – say AI changed the substance and stability of their jobs overnight. They worry about AI jeopardizing their cognitive abilities, contributing to climate change, undermining value to customers and compromising security. Some, like Sharma, have left their fields entirely, shifting to vastly different careers.

So far, economic data shows that AI has not wreaked havoc on the workforce. It’s created about 1m US jobs, compared with 200,000 layoffs attributed to AI, according to the Economist . But as AI executives continue to warn of disruption, 71% of Americans believe the technology will lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years, according to the Pew Research Center . As workers fear for the future, though, they’re making major decisions about the present.

Some white-collar workers have begun to look beyond the dreams they were sold as AI reshapes jobs.

After spending nearly a decade in public relations, 30-year-old Vanessa Hsia decided to seek a master’s degree in comparative literature.

“I felt very burnt out and concerned with the direction of the industry: chasing quantity over quality, relying on AI rather than critical thinking, prioritizing short-term wins over long-term strategy,” Hsia posted on LinkedIn . “I have no idea where this path will lead, but I’m taking my own advice: the world is on fire, might as well do what you want.”

Hsia and her former colleagues in PR feared AI would eventually replace them, she said, noting that specific tasks like pitching reporters over email were already being automated.

“I’ve been sold this dream that if I work really hard in my career, I’ll climb the ladder, that I will be respected in my field and paid a fair wage,” she said. “But then you have this technology that exacerbates the fact that, actually, no, that’s not guaranteed.”

The safe, tidy way of life defined by a bachelor’s degree, desk job and career ladder is in its death throes, accelerated by the encroaching tidal wave of AI, Hsia contends. It’s an opinion echoed by other white-collar workers.

“The career that I’ve had for 10 years is kind of fundamentally gone,” said a software engineer at a big tech company, who requested anonymity for fear of retribution. The engineer and his peers believe their roles will soon cease to exist as AI automates coding. “We all thought we would be software engineers for another decade or two,” he said, adding that he’s considering leaving the industry. “Now it’s completely changed.”

For some workers, AI has accelerated feelings of instability and purposelessness they already had in their careers. Hanna Horvath spent most of her twenties as a content marketer and editor. But earlier this year, the 29-year-old left her editing job at personal finance platform Bankrate to freelance in copy writing and social media marketing, serve as a financial planner and publish a Substack newsletter.

Even before the introduction of AI, Horvath felt like her day-to-day work had drifted away from what she was hired to do, becoming “meaningless”. And after witnessing multiple layoffs at her company, she no longer felt assured by the promised stability of a nine-to-five job.

Once her company mandated AI use, Horvath felt even worse. “AI doesn’t have to replace your job to fundamentally change your relationship to your job,” she said. “So many of us were just becoming project managers instead of actually editing content or writing content.”

On LinkedIn , Horvath wrote that though the larger conversation about AI has been about job displacement, the tech “has already changed worker psychology”, referring to people’s fears and loss of purpose. Now, with varied streams of income, Horvath said she feels more financially secure and less vulnerable to AI replacement.

Some white-collar workers are effecting complete professional 180s: from tech to law enforcement and advertising to acting.

Chris, who asked to go by a pseudonym for fear of retribution, left his software engineering job to join the police department of a major east coast city last year. AI had taken “a lot of the thinking” and fun out of coding, and he feared being displaced, he said.

“There’s no job security in corporate anymore,” said Chris, who spent more than a decade doing white-collar work. “You’re expendable, you’re an asset.”

Chris counts himself lucky to have left software engineering as his employer started to push AI on his team. Now, as a police officer, “there’s a satisfaction I never got in engineering … In a lot of ways I am happier,” he said, referring to working directly with his community.

Similarly, Kara, who asked to go by a pseudonym to speak candidly about her former career, said leaving her job as an advertising producer to focus on acting while moonlighting as a barista made her “feel spiritually lighter”.…

title: Yankees 2026 Roster Report Cards: Fernando Cruz
author: Jonathan Farrar
text:
Fernando Cruz was having a solid campaign before a partial UCL tear brought his 2026 season to an end.

One of the most beautiful parts of baseball is how many different personal journeys we fans get to learn about as players chase their dreams. Fernando Cruz’s story aside, let’s dive into the season that earned him a B- from the staff here at Pinstripe Alley.

Cruz’s 2026 really started at the World Baseball Classic, representing Team Puerto Rico. After rejoining the Yankees, he picked up where he left off last season as a trusted member of Aaron Boone’s bullpen. From there, it became a story of two halves.

2026 Stats: 61 games, 54.2 IP, 3.13 ERA (135 ERA+), 4.17 FIP, 4.39 xFIP, 28.6 K%, 13.7 BB%, 0.0 fWAR, 1.2 rWAR, 4-6 record

2027 Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible

Before the All-Star break, Cruz was excellent. He was a borderline All-Star, striking out 50 batters over 40 innings while holding opponents to a .191 batting average. His best month of the season was May, when he appeared in 14 games and posted a 1.02 WHIP while allowing just two earned runs over 13.2 innings. He was one of the more dependable pieces out of the bullpen during the first half of what was an underrated unit.

The key to this effectiveness was his splitter, which he deployed 51.3 percent of the time. He paired that pitch with a four-seamer, sweeper, and sinker to keep hitters off-balance. The splitter continued to be his best weapon, generating a 52 percent whiff rate and limiting hitters to a .161 average against it.

After the break, however, his performance began to slip. Something seemed off as Cruz started losing some control in late July, and August became his roughest month of the season. He posted a 6.75 ERA over eight innings, allowing six home runs and four walks. Following a blown save against Houston on August 25th, the Yankees announced that Cruz had suffered a partial tear of his right ulnar collateral ligament, and he landed on the injured list the following day.

The ultimate team guy, Cruz opted to pursue a non-surgical approach after receiving a second opinion with the hope he could make it back in 2026. He received a cortisone shot and started rehabbing trying to find his way back into the mix for the postseason. However, a month after landing on the injured list, the Yankees transferred Cruz to the 60-day injured list on September 25th, ending his chances of returning during the 2026 season.

On the season, Cruz had some impressive underlying numbers. He ranked in the 91st percentile in average exit velocity and the 99th percentile in whiff rate. He also landed in the 82nd percentile in xERA, the 88th percentile in strikeout rate, and the 85th percentile in extension. However, his hard-hit rate ranked in just the 22nd percentile, and his walk rate was in the third percentile. The right-hander was also effective against left-handed hitters holding them to a .180 batting average.

Losing Cruz after the Trade Deadline was less than ideal, especially with the Yankees having few options capable of replacing his production internally, which led to the Michael Fulmer experience. As the page turns to a new season, with the injury question mark hovering over him, Cruz becomes an interesting offseason decision for the Yankees.

The team has until November 20th to tender him a contract for the 2027 season. Depending on the outlook for his elbow, it would not surprise me to see the Yankees retain him and try to work out a deal before arbitration. Given the injury uncertainty, it could be a buy-low opportunity for the club, provided they believe he can return to form and he is willing to accept a similar salary to last season. However, professional baseball is a business and the team might opt to use the money and roster spot they would spend on Cruz elsewhere this offseason.

Personally, I gave Cruz a B for this season, and in hindsight, I feel that might have been a touch low. What grade would you assign Cruz, and what are your thoughts on him in pinstripes in 2027?

See more of the Yankees Roster Report Card series here .

title: No more Cybertrucks; Musk moves on from the angular metallic flop
author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
text:
Elon’s Edsel is no more. Last night, Tesla CEO Elon Musk revealed on social media that his car company is ending its failed attempt to wrest control of the American pickup truck market. The Cybertruck will cease production in the middle of 2027, liberating that space in Tesla’s cavernous factory for other uses—more Cybercabs , most likely.

Musk first revealed the Cybertruck in late 2019 , back when Tesla was still trading at a theoretically understandable price-to-earning ratio. The pickup's unusual angular shape owed more to low-res video game models than any concessions to practicality. At the time, Musk made fanciful claims that the truck would use a stainless steel monocoque construction, telling his audience that “the body and bed don’t do anything useful” on a normal truck. While some race cars use carbon-fiber monocoques for strength and lightness, making a pickup truck with a stainless steel monocoque chassis would only make sense if someone had an awful lot of stainless steel lying around and needed something to do with it all.

The truck was supposed to go on sale for less than $40,000, and Tesla made its usual stratospheric sales predictions that (had they been accurate) the bare metal EVs would be as ubiquitous as the Model 3 and Y.

title: Commuters and shoppers face disruption from tube driver strikes in run-up to Christmas
author: Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent
text:
RMT union calls eight 24-hour strikes on London Underground in opposition to plans for four-day week

Tube train drivers in the RMT union have called eight 24-hour strikes running over 16 days – including six in the lead-up to Christmas – that threaten to bring transport chaos to the capital.

The drivers will start another series of 24-hour strikes in late November in opposition to plans for a four-day week – a proposal that has been warmly welcomed by the majority of London Underground drivers represented by the Aslef union.

Disruption could mean few tube trains over the last shopping weekend before Christmas, with strikes running from noon on Thursday 17 December and again on Saturday 19 December.

The 24-hour strikes will begin at noon on 26 November, followed by the Christmas industrial action, with two more strikes planned in early January and more in February.

The RMT claims the new four-day week, which Transport for London (TfL) has said would be voluntary, would “undermine existing agreements and worsen working conditions”.

Previous strikes earlier this year resulted in widespread disruption to London Underground services, although trains ran on most lines.

The RMT said it has yet to receive guarantees about drivers’ right to remain on existing five-day working arrangements. It believes the proposals would worsen shift times and certainty.

The RMT’s general secretary, Eddie Dempsey, said: “London Underground is attempting to dress up a wholesale attack on drivers’ working conditions as a voluntary four-day week.

“Our members are being asked to spend more time driving trains, accept longer and more unpredictable shifts and surrender agreements that have been negotiated and defended over many years.

“This is not about improving work-life balance. It is about squeezing more work out of fewer drivers while giving management greater flexibility at the expense of our members.”

Similar, highly disruptive strikes took place in London in April and June, despite TfL insisting the proposals were completely voluntary, and the plans having been fully endorsed by the main drivers union, Aslef.

title: US job growth exceeds expectations in October despite economic uncertainty
author: Lauren Aratani in New York
text:
‘Low-hire, low-fire’ labor market shows sluggish growth but few layoffs, with an interest rate hike expected in December

The US added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October, a sign of resilience in the labor market amid ongoing war in the Middle East and inflation, according to new data released on Friday.

Economists had said the labor market has been stuck in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, in which job growth is sluggish but layoffs also remain low, but October’s data surpassed economist expectations. The unemployment rate went down slightly to 4.1%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.

Average hourly earnings increased at an annual rate of 3.1%, slightly higher than last month. Inflation over the last few months has largely outpaced the growth in wages – what often leads people to feel they are spending even more to buy essentials. In September, the annualized inflation rate was 3.7%.

Initial figures for August and September were also revised up by a total of 84,000 jobs. Job growth was seen in healthcare, transportation, warehousing and manufacturing.

Other data released earlier this week showed employment has been steady. Layoffs in September fell to their lowest level in a year and a half, according to the bureau, while outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas tracked just under 44,000 layoffs in October – a 71% decrease compared with last October.

The new data comes after a seismic midterm election that solidified Democrats’ control of Congress for the next two years. Multiple polls had shown Americans were most frustrated about the state of the economy, especially higher gas and grocery prices.

“Americans delivered a clear verdict in the midterm elections that the current economy is squeezing people financially and making it hard to get by, let alone get ahead,” said Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union, in a statement before Friday’s report. “The labor market is a good example of why people are frustrated.”

But it’s unclear when Americans will get relief. Gas prices are on average $1 a gallon higher than they were a year ago because of the war in Iran. The price of diesel, which is used throughout the supply chain to power large vehicles, is 60% higher compared with prewar levels.

In times of stubborn inflation, the US Federal Reserve usually intervenes by raising interest rates, which slows price increases. In September, the Fed hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023, bringing them up to a range of 3.75%-4%, citing inflation. Though officials kept rates steady at their last meeting in October, held the week before the election, economists are expecting one more rate hikes at the next central bank meeting in December.

Meanwhile, markets over the last week have been shaken as investors appeared worried about AI spending. After reaching correction territory, when an index drops 10% below its most recent peak, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index briefly made a recovery on Wednesday before diving back into correction territory on Thursday.

title: Rocket Report: Artemis II literally tore through the atmosphere; New Glenn delay
author: Stephen Clark
text:
Welcome to Edition 9.18 of the Rocket Report! Blue Origin packed a lot of news into one afternoon Thursday with the reveal of a new kick stage for the New Glenn rocket, a new rocket engine design, and the minor and widely expected delay for New Glenn's return-to-flight mission from December until January. The reconstruction of Blue Origin's wrecked launch pad at Cape Canaveral, Florida, continues apace after a catastrophic explosion nearly six months ago. There's a lot of pent-up demand from NASA, Amazon, and the Space Force for Blue Origin to get New Glenn back in action.

As always, we welcome reader submissions , and if you don't want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.

SpaceX vets work on water-fed propulsion . Three brothers who worked at SpaceX in the Falcon 9 era are now building satellites that run on water, a potentially harvestable resource on the Moon and found all over the Solar System, Ars reports . In late 2022, the three Carlisle brothers founded Argo Space to build infrastructure in space. Their vision was not just in-space transportation but also removing the need to use propellants from Earth to move around the heavens. Argo Space's satellites will use water not only as a propellant, but also as a coolant and radiation shield.

title: Flávio Bolsonaro battles to remain relevant as he speaks at rightwing conference at Mar-a-Lago
author: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro
text:
Far-right politician addresses Conservative Political Action Conference and makes unsubstantiated claims about election fraud

Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right politician who lost Brazil’s presidential election last month, has insisted his defeat is not “the end for Brazil” as he battles to maintain political relevance after fleeing to the US.

Bolsonaro absconded early last week shortly after losing the 25 October election to the leftwing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than 4m votes.

On Thursday night Bolsonaro made his first major public appearance since arriving in the US, speaking at a rightwing gathering at Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property where he claimed “great things” were still to come.

“I know this wasn’t the end for Brazil and I know it wasn’t the end for America,” Bolsonaro, 45, told a gala dinner at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC)’s four-day “gathering of visionaries” event, where the former British prime minister Liz Truss is also due to speak.

“Even when what seems like the end isn’t what we’d hoped for, we must thank God and have even more faith that this isn’t yet the end,” he added. “No one shuts the door that he opens – and the door he shuts, no one opens.”

Earlier, in his first post-election interview, Bolsonaro made a series of unsubstantiated claims about election fraud and insisted he received “help from absolutely no one” to flee.

“It was all me,” Bolsonaro told the New York Times , contradicting reports that he was helped by the Trump adviser Jason Miller and Santiago Caputo, a close aide to Argentina’s rightwing president, Javier Milei.

He said he would “take to the grave” the full story of how he had fled Brazil, where he faces federal police investigations for money laundering and corruption. Bolsonaro is a member of congress who has held elected office for more than 20 years but he will lose parliamentary immunity early next year when his term ends, meaning he could then be prosecuted.

Brazilian analysts agree that by skipping the country after an election in which he received 59m votes, Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro , abdicated leadership of the opposition and sabotaged his political future.

Thomas Traumann, an author and pundit for the TV network GloboNews, said: “Flávio was foolish enough to throw away the leadership of the opposition that he could have exercised had he stayed in Brazil. But the [Bolsonaro] family is still a player.”

Flávio Bolsonaro’s brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, also lives in self-imposed exile in the US and will have to serve a four-year sentence for coercion if he returns to Brazil. Four other members of the Bolsonaro family were elected to congress in last month’s election, including their brothers Carlos and Jair Renan and stepmother, Michelle Bolsonaro.

Traumann believed it was not inconceivable that Jair Bolsonaro would attempt a political comeback if he managed to negotiate his way out of his 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. However, as things stand, the 71-year-old is banned from running for office until 2060 and must live under house arrest.

Many doubt the Bolsonaro family can continue to control Bolsonarismo, the populist political movement that takes their name, with two key members in exile and one imprisoned.

“[The movement] is mortally wounded because of its mistakes and its crimes,” the political scientist Sérgio Abranches told the newspaper O Globo this week.

Abranches said democratic rightwing politicians now had a chance to “detach” themselves from the Bolsonaros’ anti-democratic movement and break off in a new direction before the next presidential election in 2030.

Flávio Bolsonaro told the New York Times he would “obviously” be a candidate in future elections but said his future lay in the US “at least for now”.

It is unclear where Flávio Bolsonaro, who has been granted a US visa by Trump, will live. His brother Eduardo set up home in Southlake, Texas, after leaving Brazil last year – although some expect him to move after the traditionally conservative state elected the Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor in this week’s midterms.

In a video posted on CPAC’s social networks before Thursday’s event, Eduardo Bolsonaro played down the risk posed by the “blue tsunami” to their ability to stay in the US. “They [Democrats] will try [to make trouble for us] – but it’s not up to Congress … to revoke visas or citizenships,” he said.

Likening their plight to that of a female asylum seeker fleeing Iran for fear of being killed after refusing to wear a hijab , he added: “I am 100% legal – as is my brother and his family.”

title: McLaren's 2027 F1 front wing breaks cover in Brazil
author: Jon Noble
text:
McLaren’s new front wing, which will be the same concept it launches its 2027 Formula 1 car with, has been revealed at the Brazilian Grand Prix.

As part of an end-of-season push by the Woking-based squad to deliver continuous improvements to its MCL40, the squad has brought its latest upgrades to Interlagos.

This includes tweaks to its floor, an updated rear wing, but also a front wing that will form the starting point for next season’s MCL41.

The front wing is a change of concept for the team as it features many revisions across the spectrum of wing elements.

The attachment point for the main plane and the endplate has been revised to now run across the lower edge – where it marries up with the refined outboard element.

The attachment between the nose and the main plane has been adjusted to sit on the second flap now rather than the mainplane, while the new wing also features an adjustment in the height of the flap elements.

Speaking ahead of the weekend, McLaren explained that the changes delivered were about both delivering more downforce and improving car balance.

Chief technical officer of aerodynamics Peter Prodromou also made clear that these changes were the launchpad for its 2027 project.

“The season isn't over yet: these upgrades are designed to improve the car now and help us in our fight for third in the championship,” he explained.

“While the learning we take from these upgrades will feed into next year’s development, we also expect to carry over the concept of the new front wing into the launch specification of next year’s car.”

title: The Traka Goes Global in Major Gravel Racing Shakeup
author: ahood
text:
The Traka World Series is a new format with seven events. (Photo: Gruber Images)

The Traka is taking its flagship brand beyond Girona and putting its stamp on a new gravel racing circuit.

Organizer Klassmark will launch The Traka World Series in 2027 to replace the Gravel Earth Series , officials announced .

The new project will include seven rounds, with equal prize money for women and men, and the promise of live broadcasts.

The series is built around growing Traka brand, and will leave several familiar stops from the Gravel Earth Series outside the new-look format.

Stages races Migration Gravel Race and Oregon Trail Gravel Grinder, as well as The Hills and Ranxo Gravel are among the events absent.

The Traka debuted in 2019 in Spain’s Girona region, and has since grown into one of the marquee events on the world gravel racing calendar.

On the back of that success, promoters launched the Gravel Earth Series in 2022. It closed out its final season in 2026 with 11 events across six countries, with Specialized Off-Road teammates Mads Würtz Schmidt and Geerike Schreurs winning the elite titles.

The new slimmed-down format puts the Traka brand front and center.

The move comes after Klassmark partnered this summer with Grupo Godó , a Barcelona promoter behind the Titan Desert and Barcelona Marathon.

The biggest change for fans in 2027 could be the ability to watch live coverage for every round, though details are not finalized.

Prize money will include a series-wide purse of €76,000 (about $85,000), divided equally between women and men in the pro category.

Racing opens at Santa Vall in February. Girona’s Traka anchors the calendar on May 1, with Iowa’s CORE4 and Belgium’s The River among the later stops.

Another event outside Europe in April and a series-ending finale called The Last Dance have venues still to be confirmed.

There are few interesting twists to the new series worth mentioning.

Riders must register as either “pro” or “open” and remain in that category all season. Only pro riders will race for overall standings and prize money, but open riders will be classified in age groups in certain events.

Cross-gender drafting is banned. Pro riders cannot use headphones, phones, or radios, and outside assistance is limited to official zones. Riders may share food, water, and basic tools, but cannot swap out bicycles or other components.

Participation also counts toward future access to the headliner event, now called The Traka Girona. Riders earn one point for each “By The Traka” event completed to count toward entry for the 2028 and 2029 editions.

title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
text:
Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result

The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.

Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party .

The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.

The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.

Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.

The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.

In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts , uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.

With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.

Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.

Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.

The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.

With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs .

Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

title: Marquez quickest as Qatar MotoGP weekend kicks off
author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
text:
MotoGP championship leader Marc Marquez led the way in the opening practice session of the Qatar Grand Prix, heading Marco Bezzecchi by a tenth of a second. Marquez led virtually the entire session on the dusty Lusail track, and ended up on a 1m52.278s. He never fitted a spare rear tyre - but neither did virtually anyone else, with no incentive to use up any of the valuable rubber in the less-representative daytime session (compared to Friday afternoon practice, the sprint and the grand prix all taking place in the evening under the lights).

Fabio Di Giannantonio was third behind Marquez and Bezzecchi, four tenths down on the leader.

Pedro Acosta was fourth as the lead KTM, but his RC16 seemed to either fail or run out of fuel in the end as he had to pull over to the side of the track.

Jorge Martin, who had withdrawn from the Sepang weekend last time out due to his wrist fracture from Phillip Island, had a livelier start here, logging 16 laps and placing fifth.

With the Yamaha riders absent as the manufacturer elected to skip Qatar, a total of 18 riders took part. Honda's new stand-in Jake Dixon was last of them, after crashing on his very first flying lap.

But Dixon was just 3.1s off the pace in the end, so will have zero trouble clearing MotoGP's 105-percent pace rule for race eligibility.

There was another crash early in the session, for KTM's Brad Binder, who likewise returned to action shortly.

title: Should the Yankees non-tender Luis Gil?
author: Andrés Chávez
text:
The erratic and increasingly injury-prone righty may or may not be on the roster past Nov. 20th.

In 2024, New York Yankees right-hander Luis Gil impressed with a brilliant first half and a full campaign worthy of the American League Rookie of the Year Award. At that point, the Bombers thought they had unearthed another pitching gem, controllable for multiple years on the cheap.

A severe lat strain in 2025 and shoulder issues in 2026 have hampered his progress and affected his fastball velocity and command, though. Last year, he posted a 3.32 ERA in 57 innings, but with very ugly peripherals. This season, the wheels completely fell off. The shoulder woes limited him to 39.1 innings between the majors and the minors. He finished with a 4.61 ERA and a rough 7.12 FIP in 27.1 MLB frames, with 18 walks and 17 strikeouts.

The right-hander started to transition to a bullpen role during the season, which could actually represent his firmest, most concrete way into the team’s plans. With the non-tender deadline looming on November 20th, however, the Yankees will have to make a decision. Is holding onto Gil worth the headache? The right-hander is projected to get a modest raise in his first year of arbitration, to $2.3 million, according to MLB Trade Rumors . Money, in this case, is not the primary issue, though.

Is Gil good or promising enough to warrant a place in the team’s future plans? Well, it will entirely depend on his ability to thrive out of the bullpen, which could be both his short and long-term home.

The concept of Gil as a multi-inning reliever is certainly enticing. Potentially increased velocity and not as much wear and tear on his shoulder sound excellent for his long-term prospects, but he does have short-term goals: looking good on the mound and getting closer to that 2024 version of himself, regardless of role. He was a completely different pitcher back then:

He is currently pitching for Tigres Del Licey in the Dominican Republic League, and boasts a solid 1.50 ERA in six frames, spanning over three games. The problem? He has issued six walks against seven strikeouts. Control has never been Gil’s calling card, but anything that starts with a five next to his BB/9 stat would represent a big problem.

The Yankees would probably love to trade Gil, hoping to get something in return for his name value and the fact that he won the award for the league’s best rookie just two years ago. They are probably dangling his name in the market as we speak. If they can’t reach a deal with any team, they will need to make a decision. They can give their promising, yet erratic right-hander one last chance, probably in the bullpen, or they could choose to cut ties and not tender him a contract, making him free to sign with any squad.

Complicating matters is the fact that Gil does not have any minor league options remaining. The next time the Yankees want to remove him from their 40-man roster, they will need to put him through waivers and risk losing him for nothing. If the Yankees can’t find a deal for him, they could opt to keep him around and try the bullpen experiment full-time to see if he can give them anything there, considering that it’s an area of need at the moment. It’s hard to see him sticking over the long term unless something drastically changes, though.

title: Dream ticket? Super-rich can sleep pretty with Singapore Airlines ‘largest double bed in the sky’
author: Lauren Almeida
text:
Cabin upgrade comes as airlines compete for wealthy customers in race to the top of luxury travel

Singapore Airlines has said it will offer the “largest double bed in the sky” as part of a S$2bn (£1.2bn) cabin upgrade as super-rich passengers demand ever greater levels of luxury travel.

The first-class premium cabins will feature what the airline claims is “the largest double bed in commercial aviation”.

The bed for two people travelling together spans two adjoining seats and measures 203cm (80in) long and 152cm (60in) wide. A standard double bed mattress in the UK is 190cm long and 135cm wide.

The bed will include a mattress topper from the German luxury bedding company Paradies, a duvet and a choice of pillows.

Some business-class seats would be able to be made into a double bed, the airline said. The upgrade includes curved sliding doors to give passengers more privacy and ultra-high-definition 4K touchscreens.

A broader race to the top in luxury travel is under way, where a one-way ticket can cost upwards of £10,000. While Singapore Airlines was ranked as the world’s best overall airline by the researcher Skytrax this year, it has lost market share to rivals who have invested heavily in cabin upgrades.

In 2022, Emirates launched a fleet-wide $5bn retrofit programme, including refreshing its first-class suites with more space and updated tech. This year Air France introduced la Première, a redesigned first-class cabin, which the airline says is akin to a private jet experience. British Airways is also working on a new first-class cabin for its A380 planes.

The industry has been rocked by a rise in fuel prices this year triggered by the war in the Middle East, which has in turn pushed up air fares. However, Singapore Airlines has benefited from an increase in passengers routing their flights between Asia and Europe rather than taking connecting flights through the Gulf.

Singapore Airlines added that economy passengers would gain more leg space, as well as a new storage layout for personal items. All passengers would get upgrades to the in-flight entertainment service and an expanded meal selection, it said, and there would be onboard internet connectivity via Elon Musk’s satellite company Starlink.

The new cabins would be introduced from the second half of 2027, the airline said.

title: 'Miraculous' – Tadej Pogačar's heart rate data and sleep scores revealed in new documentary
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
Tadej Pogačar has a resting heart rate of 38 beats per minute, a heart rate variability of 100, and a 'miraculous' prowess for sleep, according to new up-to-date figures revealed by his physiological data tracking sponsor, Whoop.

The numbers were disclosed in the first of a new documentary series on Eurosport, TNT Sports and HBO Max, titled ‘Anatomy of a G.O.A.T’ , which aims to "decode the science behind the greatest athletes of all-time".

The first documentary, which airs on Saturday, looks to piece together the puzzle of Pogačar’s startling superiority over the rest of the peloton.

"Tadej’s resting heart rate, right, which is a very nice kind of global picture of your cardiorespiratory fitness, is 38," says Whoop’s Global Head of Human Performance, Kristen Holmes.

Holmes states that the average resting heart rate for a male of Pogačar’s, 27, age is 59, while also revealing that the other 27-year-old riders on UAE Team Emirates-XRG are a good bit higher.

"The average of the six other teammates is 42. He’s about four beats per minute slower than his teammates. And what this points to is a more efficient cardiorespiratory system, because he’s got this very efficient engine."

Pogačar’s resting heart rate of 38, while putting him a cut above his teammates, is not other-worldly like the 28bpm reportedly associated with another five-time Tour de France winner, Miguel Indurain.

Earlier this year, Pogačar’s top Classics rival, Mathieu van der Poel revealed his resting heart rate was the same, on average, at 38, though he noted the lowest he’d recorded was 34.

Heart rate variability – or a 'readiness indicator'

Whoop, as with Van der Poel earlier in the year, also revealed Pogačar’s heart rate variability, which is a measure of the variation in time taken between heart beats, measured in milliseconds over a long period of time, such as overnight.

It tracks the balance of the body’s autonomic nervous system but is described by Whoop in layman’s terms as a “readiness indicator”, with a higher HRV indicating superior physical fitness and recovery.

"The more variable that time interval, the more kind of ready you are to take on load," says Holmes. "So Tadej, his heart rate variability is 100. The other six riders on his team, their average is in the 80s. So he has to work less hard for the same output."

While the average HRV for active individuals is said to be between 40 and 65, Pogačar’s score of 100 pales in comparison with Van der Poel’s claimed HRV of 200.

"I’m really high in HRV," Van der Poel said earlier this year. "I think it’s a bit genetical, but fitness is important also. For sure, it’s something that makes me stronger and better recovered."

The HRV scores tie into the most important factor when it comes to recovery: sleep, and here is another area where Pogačar is said to be "remarkable". Whoop’s wearable technology monitors riders overnight, and gives them a ‘sleep score’ in the morning.

"Sleep consistency is when you go to bed and when you wake up, and the stability of that. And it’s expressed as a percentage. So on a scale of 0 to 100, again, you know, Tadej is 84%," says Holmes in the ‘Anatomy of a G.O.A.T’ documentary.

"Over the course of the 2026 Tour de France, none of the cyclists on the UAE team had sleep consistency that compared to Tadej’s 84%. They were mostly in the 70 to 80% range," adds Research Scientist Gregory Grosicki.

"One of the things we see very clearly in our data is that, when our members and even our elite athletes on Whoop do very high intensity efforts, the quality of their sleep tends to suffer. But with Tadej, he takes that even a step further. Going into the [Tour de France], he was sleeping about 7 hours. During the entire 2026 Tour de France, he was sleeping 8 hours. Miraculous. He’s sleeping more. He’s sleeping more regularly."

Asked about his sleep skills, Pogačar said: “I’m not a big hour sleeper, but if you eat clean and good for the dinner, I think it’s the biggest impact on the sleep then. And yeah, you just need to be relaxed and be organised for the next morning.”

Pogačar's powers of recovery were further underlined by his former coach Iñigo San Millán.

"He has an astonishing ability to recover," said the Spaniard. "We did some metabolic testing. We can see between 1000 and 2000 metabolic parameters, and one of them is ability to recover. Some of the antioxidant parameters are very important for recovery. When we saw his results, Tadej was far ahead of everyone else."

title: How much has bad luck really cost George Russell in F1 2026?
author: Josh Suttill
text:
George Russell says he's only had six race weekends without an issue in a bruising 2026 Formula 1 season.

But, on a Brazilian Grand Prix weekend where he's facing another grid penalty , does his claim stack up, and how much does bad luck explain his clear defeat to Kimi Antonelli?

Antonelli has destroyed his Mercedes team-mate Russell this year, winning nine races to Russell's three and wrapping up the title with four rounds to spare last weekend in Mexico.

Facing the media for the first time in Brazil since that crushing title loss was confirmed, Russell admitted to "feel[ing] a bit exhausted this season of constantly picking myself back up".

"When you get kicked to the ground, you pick yourself back up, then you get kicked down again, you pick yourself back up, and I was hoping to do that maybe twice in the season, not every other weekend really," he said.

"When you get to a point of this season, you're away from home three weeks in a row, and you have another race like what happened in Mexico, where a chance of victory, a chance of the podium, just disappears totally outside of your control, it's tough to deal with. It's very tough to deal with.

"So Brazil's a place that I love, I've got great memories of. Do I come in with high expectations? Honestly, no, to be honest. But looking forward to next year for sure. And just continue to work on the things that I can control, and pray that things outside of my control sort themselves out."

Russell said he went through every race of 2026 with his engineers and found "we've only had six races this season where we had not an issue".

"So 14 [likely 13, as there have been 19 weekends so far] of those races we've had things that have been what we thought was bad luck, but we need to start questioning things more deeply when it's happening so often, and especially on our side.

"That was the main feeling for me."

So, we put that claim to the test: we've gone through F1 2026's 19 weekends so far and found the following:

Russell's campaign started in dream fashion with a dominant victory in the Australian season opener, while Antonelli paid the price for a costly final practice crash that left him compromised for the rest of the weekend on a suboptimal, unrefined set-up.

He could probably still count Australia as an 'issue' weekend as he had to fight back from having a depleted battery before he started the race - costing him positions to the Ferraris and requiring him to fight back into the lead.

Russell followed it up with a sprint win in China, but his first real bit of bad luck came in grand prix qualifying when his car ground to a halt at the start of Q3. This left him needing a late lap to salvage second on the grid.

Reflecting on that session, Russell told media including The Times : "I pulled the clutch half a second too early in the qualifying, which led to my car breaking down.

"Should we have known about that? Maybe yes. Maybe not."

Russell had been faster than Antonelli all the way through the weekend up to that point, so you can make a case he'd have won there with a normal Q3.

At Suzuka, poor safety car timing helped Antonelli to victory and cost Russell a shot at it. But Antonelli looked the faster driver and may have won on sheer pace. It looked more like a fight between him and Oscar Piastri's McLaren .

But Russell was also then further compromised on the safety car restart by his car being put into an extra harvesting mode, leaving him fourth at the chequered flag.

"Then in Japan, doing the upshift at the exact same time as I clicked another button...on the steering wheel...should we have known about that? Maybe yes. Maybe not," Russell reflected.

Antonelli won from pole in Miami while Russell finished fourth on what appeared to be a clean weekend for both cars.

Russell and Antonelli then scrapped for victory in Canada when Russell's engine failed while he was leading.

Antonelli won again in Monaco while Russell had a double-hit of penalties, the latter for Mercedes not serving his first, a five-second penalty for pitlane speeding, correctly.

Given the circumstances of the pitlane speed limit penalties that weekend and Russell being blameless for the second penalty, it was another unlucky weekend and a lost podium (as he was third on the late-race restart).

Russell finished second at Barcelona; Antonelli had passed him (and may have challenged Lewis Hamilton for the victory), but his Mercedes broke down with an electrical issue late on.

Russell won in Austria, beautifully judging the yellow flags in qualifying while Antonelli mistook double-waved yellows for single ones and backed off, ending up fourth on the grid and third in the race.

Russell struggled with power unit deployment issues at Silverstone and Spa. At Silverstone he salvaged second (so probably did not lose any points) while Antonelli loses a likely victory to a front-left wheel-shield failure. At Spa, the issue cost Russell 0.2-0.25 seconds in qualifying, while on the opening lap it left him vulnerable on the Kemmel Straight.

This led to contact with Lewis Hamilton, who was penalised for the collision - which put Russell out on the spot. Antonelli won the race from pole.

At Hungary, Russell cracked a sump running slightly wide over a kerb in Q3, which left him seventh on the grid prompted engine-swap ramifications down the line. Then in the race he stalled and sank like a stone because of an engine rev anomaly, and an ill-timed virtual safety car stunted his recovery, while Antonelli took third.

Antonelli and Russell finished second and third at Zandvoort, while at Monza Antonelli's excellent charge through the field - from 19th, owing to an engine-change grid penalty - was aided by the red flag and another well-timed virtual safety car.

Antonelli's pace was so strong he may have still won without those anyway, but he was certainly aided by fortune on Sunday.

A virtual safety car helped Antonelli beat Lando Norris's McLaren to victory in Madrid while Russell was fifth, off Antonelli's pace all weekend.

Russell won in Baku while Antonelli crashed in qualifying before recovering to fifth.

Another power unit failure at Sepang cost Russell a likely podium meant he had to take a grid penalty in Singapore. Russell blew a sprint victory there by crashing out of the lead at the end of the first lap, while he recovered to ninth in the grand prix.

Russell picked up a five-second time penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage at Austin and labelled his own pace "rubbish" en route to eighth, while Antonelli won again.

Then in Antonelli's title-sealing Mexico weekend, Russell had a deployment issue that dropped him from his front-row start. He clashed with Isack Hadjar's Red Bull and was penalised 10 seconds.

So really, there have been 12 weekends where Russell has some publicly disclosed bad luck - 10 of which cost him points - not counting issues that he or the team have not revealed. It is true that this dwarfs Antonelli's misfortune, as he only really lost points to factors outside his control at Silverstone and Barcelona.

Ultimately, Russell can only make a case that he lost victories in China (Q3 problem), Canada (power unit failure) and Monza (red flag and VSC timing that helped Antonelli), but even all three of those were far from guaranteed. Maybe Antonelli would've just been quicker even if Russell had a normal qualifying in China, maybe Antonelli would've won their dogfight in Canada, and maybe Antonelli had the pace at Monza to win regardless.

We'll never know the answer to those questions, but only the most ludicrously generous estimates of the points Russell has lost this season put him marginally ahead of Antonelli right now, if you then subtract the points Antonelli gains from it.

Russell's lost points to bad luck - A (very) generous view

China - 7 points (1st not 2nd) Japan - 6 points (2nd not 4th) Montreal - 25 points (1st not DNF)

Monaco - 15 points (3rd not 12th) Belgium - 15 points (3rd not DNF)

Hungary - 6 points (4th not 7th) Italy - 7 points (1st not 2nd)

Malaysia - 15 points (3rd not 20th) Singapore - 6 points (6th not 9th)

Mexico - 10 points (2nd not 6th)

Total = 112 lost points New gap to Antonelli = Russell leads by 6 points

*accounting for Antonelli's net points loss as a result

This would be an impossibly fortunate season for Russell, taking very generous liberties such as assuming he wins in China, Canada and Italy, plus presuming he maintains his second place in Mexico, and crucially not removing of Antonelli's own bad luck.

And even in this highly unlikely scenario where Russell is leading by six points, you'd back Antonelli to overturn it comfortably in the final four races on this season's form.

In reality, even if you balanced out the reliability dramas of both cars, of which Russell has had more, Russell would still be over 60 points behind Antonelli instead of 130.

Russell called it "difficult to put a number on how much [reliability] has impacted the championship" and pointed to one important factor.

"It's often about momentum. When we start the season, we had the issue in China with the failure in qualifying, we had the issues in Japan, we had the engine failure in Canada, we had the drivethrough penalty that wasn't a drivethrough penalty in Monaco. These things compound," Russell explained.

"If you're in the championship fight, or you're within touching distance, you don't feel like you're having to do catch-up. And maybe that contributed towards overdriving and trying to overachieve. Maybe not."

Again, we'll never know how a cleaner start to the season would've changed things for Russell or put more pressure on Antonelli. Russell's bigger problem was how quickly Antonelli became the faster Mercedes driver.

Has Russell had more bad luck than Antonelli this year? Yes. But has Antonelli been the better, faster driver on more weekends? Absolutely yes.

And it's something Russell himself acknowledged in Mexico on the eve of Antonelli's coronation: "The truth is he's been at a higher level than me this year."

The bad luck ballooned the gap and made the defeat all the more crushing, but the speed and execution difference this year meant the intra-team fight was only ever going one way.

title: EF Education-EasyPost continue post-Carapaz rebuild for 2027 with two more development team graduates
author: James Moultrie
text:
The former had started his path to the pros in Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe's junior setup at Team GRENKE-Auto Eder, but joined EF Education-Aevolo for 2026. Despite setbacks due to crashes and injury in the first half of the season, Capello closed out the racing calendar strongly and has now earned the step up he's dreamed of.

They join Tao Geoghegan Hart, Ivan Sosa, Nicholas Milesi, Tobias Bayer, and Emil Herzog as EF's new arrivals for 2027. Team boss Jonathan Vaughters had already confirmed that Carapaz's departure was due to overstretched finances , with development team graduates allowing them to bolster their roster size closer to the 30-rider maximum while keeping the costs down

"I’m looking forward to the future and not looking back. It’s been my dream to race pro since I started cycling. I can’t wait to race with the best riders in the world, and EF Education-EasyPost is a really cool group," said Capello.

"I’ve had my fair share of bad luck this season, but I’m confident I’m in a good position to join the WorldTour with EF Education-EasyPost. They have shown a lot of patience and faith in my qualities as a rider, and I’ve worked really hard since joining the development team at the start of the year. I’m confident I can have a successful 2027 with the team and be a strong rider and teammate.

"Next year I want to try my hand at some short stage races but mostly just gain as much experience as possible. I want to learn from my teammates, and give everything that I can. I can’t wait to start."

His best results so far came as a junior in 2025, taking second at the European Championships road race, sixth in the World Championships time trial, and winning the Italian junior ITT title. Despite the injuries, which mostly prevented him from kicking on fully in 2026, EF are still confident in his abilities as a GC prospect.

"If you see Roberto’s results, he was one of the top riders in 2025. I’m super happy that we signed him," said head of scouting Sebastian Langeveld.

"This year was a bit on and off because of injury, but you can see from his training that he’s super talented. He has an incredible capacity on climbs and against the clock. He’s a very promising GC rider. It will take time, maybe a few years, but he has the qualities even though he’s still super young."

Hlady rode as a stagiaire for the WorldTour squad back at the end of 2024, and then raced for two seasons on the Aevolo squad to earn his way up to a full spot. A two-time under-23 national road race champion , Hlady also finished on the podium of the elite men's road race at the US national champs in 2025 behind Quinn Simmons and Evan Boyle.

"I’m excited to be stepping up and into the next phase of my career with this amazing team," said Hlady.

"Honestly, over the last few years, I always thought joining the WorldTour was possible, but I never thought it was guaranteed, so having this opportunity means so much to me. I truly believe that I have more to give and more room to develop as a rider."

In 2026, he finished second on a stage of the Alpes Isère Tour, and netted top-10s on stages at the Flèche du Sud and Le Tour de Bretagne Cycliste. For 2027, Hlady is looking to improve on his versatility, with the team confident he can go in any direction when it comes to specialising.

"Obviously, EF Education-EasyPost has strong American roots, but even if you took that aspect out of the equation, this is the team that I’d want to join. If you lined up all the teams in the men’s WorldTour, I’d choose EF Education-EasyPost every time," he said.

"I’m grateful, and I appreciate that we still have this cool international flavour and culture. I think we’re a really diverse team, and what sets us apart is that at the biggest races we always seem to punch above our weight. It’s an all-or-nothing and fun racing attitude. From the outside, they seem like the best team too because all the staff seem really cool too," he added.

"I want to get stronger, better and faster in every possible way and then see where that takes me. From there, I’ll sit down with the team in November at our next camp, and that’s when we’ll formulate a plan in terms of expectations and race calendar."

"Gavin came with Aevolo, and he’s shown throughout the last couple of years, with his national titles, that he has a lot of upward potential. He raced with the WorldTour team this year, and he did really well as a teammate, and he’s ticked a lot of boxes for us this year," added Langeveld.

"It’s a bit early to determine where he will end up as a rider, but he still has a lot of untapped potential, and we’re going to work with him on getting the best out of himself in the coming season. He can climb, and he might even go in the direction of the classics, but really, it’s about taking our time with the young riders and not rushing them."

title: Permane to stay as Racing Bulls team principal
text:
Red Bull have extended Alan Permane's contract as boss of their second team until the end of 2031.

The 59-year-old Englishman was promoted from racing director to team principal of Racing Bulls in July 2025, when predecessor Laurent Mekies was moved to the same role at Red Bull following the sacking of Christian Horner.

The team secured their first podium finish in four years at last season's Dutch Grand Prix with Isack Hadjar, and this season are fifth in the championship - the leading outfit behind the 'big four' - after 19 races.

Oliver Mintzlaff, who runs Red Bull's F1 programme as chief executive officer of corporate projects and investments, said: "Alan is doing a tremendous job, and the progress the team has made is a direct reflection of his experience, commitment and competitive mindset.

"He brings clarity, composure, and a deep understanding of what it takes to perform in Formula 1, while creating an environment where people can consistently deliver at their best.

"The results Racing Bulls has achieved in recent seasons underline the strength of the team and the work being done throughout the organisation.

"Alan has played a key role in that progress, and we are very pleased that he will continue to lead the team as we look to build on this momentum in the years ahead."

Before joining Red Bull, Permane spent 34 years at the team based in Enstone in Oxfordshire through various guises as Benetton, Renault and Lotus, winning two world titles each with Michael Schumacher and Fernando Alonso.

He said: "I am immensely proud to be continuing this journey and I would like to thank everyone at Red Bull for the trust and support they have given me.

"What makes this team special is the shared spirit of everyone; trackside, in Faenza and in Milton Keynes, and it is a privilege to lead such a talented and committed group every day.

"Fighting for fifth in the championship is something we should all be very proud of, but it is the result of years of hard work from a lot of people, and we are not done yet.

"We have the right people, the right culture and a clear sense of where we want to go, and I am excited to keep pushing together."

title: Michael Vanthourenhout fined for post-race clash with Cameron Mason at Middelkerke cyclo-cross
author: Owen Rogers
text:
Round two of the Superprestige ended in controversy on Thursday evening after series leader Michael Vanthourenhout (Pauwels-Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw) was fined following a post-race altercation.

The incident occurred after he clashed with Cameron Mason (777TV) late in the Superprestige race at Middelkerke, the Belgian rider shoulder barging Mason on the eighth of 10 laps of the Nordzeecross circuit.

After the race, Vanthourenhout was seen on TV coverage approaching and shouting at Mason, who turned round and remonstrated with the Belgian, the two arguing briefly. Organisers have confirmed to that Vanthourenhout was fined 200 Swiss francs (€218) for the post-race incident.

Vanthourenhout had led onto the eighth lap, but was in second place behind eventual winner Joran Wyseure when Mason made a move on a straight section. Seeing the Scottish rider coming up on his left, Vanthourenhout moved out and barged into him, but in doing so seemed to be concentrating too much on Mason and not on the race, losing balance and crashing on the next left hand bend.

Consequently, Vanthourenhout dropped back to seventh place and was forced to chase back to the leading group. Meanwhile, Mason also crashed, after failing to negotiate a set of barriers, falling from second to sixth place, Vanthourenhout clearly commenting to the Scot as he passed, pushing him wide on the next bend.

"It was in the heat of the battle, adrenaline got the better of us," Vanthourenhout said in his post-race interview.

"I don't think he should have come on the inside there, but it is a manoeuvre that is allowed. I lost my balance, and from sixth or seventh place it is difficult to get to the front."

When asked whether the incident prevented him winning he said: "It plays a role, but that is a race. I was disappointed, but I am also happy that I still made the podium. My second place is good for the standings."

For his part, Mason was seen laughing with team staff after the incident, later adding the caption "Something something, 'own medicine' something something. Another solid race. Onto the next" on his Instagram story.

The race was a fast one with hectic, exciting racing throughout, Joran Wyseure (Crelan-Corendon) taking the win ahead of Vanthourenhout. Swiss champion Kevin Kuhn (Heizomat-Cube) was third, one place ahead of Mason.

Vanthourenhout has had an excellent start to the season, winning four of his seven races to date and never finishing off the podium. Having won the first round of the Superprestige at Overijse on October 25, he started Thursday’s race leading the series, his second place enough to retain his lead in a series where he finished second overall last season.

Though not matching his Belgian rival, Mason has also had a good season, with eighth place in the first of six races the lowest placing so far. The two riders will line up against each other at Sunday's European championships, which Vanthourenhout won ahead of Mason in 2023.
